candidates.name: Chris Hill
candidates.current_role: Collin County Judge since 2019
candidates.background: Chris Hill was first elected Collin County Judge in 2018 and is seeking a third term. He previously served as Collin County Commissioner for Precinct 3. He is a certified public accountant with degrees from Texas A&M University-Commerce, the University of Texas at Dallas, Webster University, and Columbia Biblical Seminary, and has worked as a corporate controller and an executive pastor. He lives in Collin County, where he says five generations of his family have lived.

priorities.text: Campaigns on the promise he says he first made of limited government, low taxes, and excellence in every aspect of county government.
Says he champions private property rights, limited regulation, and government transparency.
Points to his COVID-era record, summarized as no lockdowns, no closures, no mask mandates, and no vaccine mandates.
Says Collin County has one of the lowest county property tax rates in Texas.
Supports regional transportation planning and infrastructure coordination.

promises.text: Pledges to keep his promises and keep the county successful if re-elected to four more years.

record.text: On Sept. 14, 2026, he cast the lone vote against the county's $619.6 million fiscal 2026-27 budget and a tax rate of $0.151414 per $100 valuation, the county's first rate increase since 1993; both passed 4-1.

Before the September 2026 vote, his motion to cut each department's budget by 2.76 percent to avoid a rate increase failed, as did his motion to lower the employee pay target from the 75th to the 50th percentile of comparison counties.
In September 2026 he was the lone vote against an elected officials' compensation plan that included raises for him and the four commissioners.

On Aug. 25, 2025, he and Commissioner Cheryl Williams voted against the total tax rate and the maintenance and operations rate for fiscal 2025-26, and he also voted against the debt service rate; the rate stayed at $0.149343.
On July 31, 2024, he cast the lone vote against the proposed fiscal 2025 combined tax rate of $0.149343, which passed 4-1.

At a June 9, 2025 meeting he directed staff to plan a move to hand-marked paper ballots after a federal executive order on barcode tabulation; on June 23, 2025 the court unanimously approved about $2.3 million in equipment.
On March 24, 2020, he issued a seven-day COVID-19 stay-at-home order that, unlike many Texas orders, allowed businesses following social distancing rules to remain open.
As a county commissioner in May 2017, he made the motion, approved 4-0, to deny further invoice payments to the court-appointed special prosecutors in the Ken Paxton securities case.

On Aug. 10, 2026, the Commissioners Court voted 4-0, with Commissioner Duncan Webb absent, to call an $817.5 million bond election for Nov. 3, 2026, choosing the larger of two final options; with four members present, the unanimous vote included Hill.
On Feb. 23, 2026, he voted with a 5-0 majority to approve a consent agenda that included a construction change order for the jail's medical and mental health expansion.

In August 2021 the Commissioners Court, which he presides over, voted to commit all of the county's roughly $201 million in federal ARPA funds to three public health capital projects, including a medical and mental health infirmary at the county jail; the court documents reviewed do not record his individual vote.

In January 2022 the Commissioners Court approved by majority vote the establishment of the Collin County Mental Health Diversion Program as a mental health specialty court; the order does not record individual votes.

In February 2024 the Commissioners Court, by majority vote with Commissioner Duncan Webb absent, awarded the construction contract for the jail's medical and mental health expansion to Sedalco, Inc.; the order does not record individual votes.

notes.text: Won the March 3, 2026 Republican primary with 78.3 percent of the vote over former Plano council member Rick Grady.
The Dallas Morning News endorsed his opponent Rick Grady in the 2026 Republican primary.

His campaign site lists endorsements from groups including Texas Right to Life, Texas Values Action, the Collin County Association of Realtors, Texas Home School Coalition PAC, and the Texas Restaurant Association.
County records describe the ARPA-funded jail medical and mental health facility as 125 beds with shell space for 136 more, at a cost of about $112 million, with opening expected in late 2026.

q_county_tax.summary: Has voted against the county tax rate in multiple budget cycles and proposed across-the-board department cuts to avoid the 2026 rate increase.

q_spending_cap.summary: KERA reported that he argued the county budget had grown faster than inflation and population combined when proposing cuts in 2026.

issue_notes.summary: KERA reported that he warned raising the tax rate in the same year the county seeks voter approval of bonds could hurt the bond's chances; the court called an $817.5 million bond election for Nov. 3, 2026.
His campaign materials, as summarized by Branch Politics, say he supports regional cooperation on mental health services.
Opposes government health mandates and says public health decisions should prioritize personal liberty.
Says he supports school choice and homeschooling communities.

On the bond, Community Impact quoted him saying residents are "going to have to pay the bill, so we want their voice on this decision," and that deferred projects are pushed into the future; Hoodline reported he favored keeping the debt service rate steady.

photo.credit: Official portrait, U.S. House of Representatives

priorities.text: Campaigns on cutting federal regulations and simplifying the tax code.
Campaigns on responsible spending and says both parties have failed to produce a balanced budget.
Calls for completing the border wall, designating certain cartels as foreign terrorist organizations and adding Border Patrol personnel.

record.text: Voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1), the 2025 budget reconciliation law that extended tax cuts and reduced projected federal Medicaid spending, on House passage in May 2025 and final passage in July 2025.
Voted for the Laken Riley Act (S. 5), which requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft-related or certain violent crimes, in January 2025.
Voted for the SAVE Act (H.R. 22), which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections, in April 2025.
Voted for the Protect Children's Innocence Act (H.R. 3492), which would make certain gender transition procedures on minors a federal crime, in December 2025.
Voted for the Do No Harm in Medicaid Act (H.R. 498), which would bar Medicaid funding for gender transition procedures for minors, in December 2025.
Voted against H.J.Res. 72, a resolution to end the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods, in February 2026.
Voted against H.R. 1834, which would extend expanded Affordable Care Act premium tax credits for three years and passed the House 230 to 196, in January 2026.
Voted for the Secure America Act (S. 2), which passed the House on a party-line vote, in June 2026.
Voted for the Born-Alive Abortion Survivors Protection Act (H.R. 21) in January 2025.
Was one of 20 Republicans who withheld their votes in the January 2023 election for Speaker to press for House rule changes, according to his campaign.
Introduced legislation to push back on executive actions on firearms during the Biden administration, according to his campaign.

q_federal_spending.summary: Voted for the 2025 reconciliation law, cites a 100 percent FreedomWorks rating and campaigns on cutting what he calls wasteful spending.

q_voting_access.summary: Voted for the SAVE Act, which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.

q_trans_minors.summary: Voted for a bill to make certain gender transition procedures on minors a federal crime and for a ban on Medicaid funding for such procedures for minors.

q_tariffs.summary: Voted against ending the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods.

q_border_state.summary: Says Texas, as a sovereign state, should increase the number of Department of Public Safety personnel on the border.

q_gun_laws.summary: Says the Second Amendment is about protecting against tyranny and opposes executive actions restricting gun rights.

q_abortion.summary: Says he will always fight to keep taxpayer dollars from funding abortion and voted for the Born-Alive bill.

issue_notes.summary: Says he has prioritized expanding U.S. energy export capacity.

candidates.current_role: Texas State Senator, District 5, since 2013
candidates.background: Schwertner is an orthopedic surgeon from Georgetown. He holds a pharmacy degree from the University of Texas at Austin and a medical degree from the University of Texas Medical Branch in Galveston. He served one term in the Texas House (District 20) before winning the Senate seat in 2012, and he chairs the Senate Business and Commerce Committee.

priorities.text: Campaigns on property tax relief and on housing affordability through infrastructure, financing options and workforce development.
Lists grid reliability, energy emergency preparedness, new power generation and nuclear energy development as priorities.
Says he supports border security funding and tools for law enforcement against cartels and human smuggling.
Says he supports teacher pay increases, career and technical education and parental control in education.
Says water infrastructure and groundwater management reform are needed, including replacing groundwater conservation district boundaries with aquifer-based authorities.

record.text: Joint author of SB 8 (2025), requiring certain sheriffs to enter 287(g) agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement; he moved adoption of its conference report, which passed 20-11.
Voted for SB 2 (2025), creating an education savings account program, and was listed as a coauthor.
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring the Ten Commandments to be displayed in public school classrooms, and was listed as a joint author.
Coauthored and voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned consumable hemp-derived THC products; Gov. Greg Abbott vetoed it.
Joint author of and voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting land purchases by people and entities tied to certain foreign countries.
Coauthored SJR 5 (2025), a constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent offenses, and voted for final Senate approval.
Joint author of and voted for SB 16 (2025), requiring proof of citizenship to register to vote; the bill did not pass the House.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the school finance bill that passed the Senate 31-0.
Voted for SB 14 (2023), banning gender transition treatments for minors.
Voted for SB 8 (2021), the law banning most abortions after cardiac activity is detected, and was listed as a joint author.
Moved adoption of the conference report on HB 1927 (2021), which allows permitless carry of handguns by adults 21 and older; it was adopted 17-13.
Voted for HB 2127 (2023), which limits city and county regulations in areas covered by state law.
Voted for SB 388 (2025), setting goals for dispatchable generation; it did not pass the House.

notes.text: In December 2018 the University of Texas at Austin closed an investigation into allegations that he sent sexually explicit messages to a graduate student, concluding the available evidence did not support a policy violation; he denied sending the messages. ATPE reports he was endorsed in the 2018 primary by the Texas Home School Coalition PAC and by Texans for Fiscal Responsibility.
Says he has been endorsed by Donald Trump, Greg Abbott and Dan Patrick.

q_abortion.summary: Joint author of and voted for SB 8 (2021); his campaign cites support for laws prohibiting abortion once a heartbeat is detected.

candidates.current_role: Texas State Representative, District 17, since 2023
candidates.background: Stan Gerdes of Smithville has represented House District 17 since 2023. He worked for more than a decade with Rick Perry, including as senior advisor during Perry's tenure as U.S. Secretary of Energy. He attended the University of Texas.

photo.credit: Official portrait, Texas House of Representatives

priorities.text: Cites work on the 2023 property tax cut, border security funding, rural law enforcement funding and the Texas Water Fund.
Lists protecting the right to life among his priorities.

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on its April 2025 House passage vote.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the House school finance and teacher pay bill.
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025), the final version of the school finance bill.
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring display of the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), the constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent felony charges.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned consumable hemp-derived THC products (later vetoed by the governor).
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting purchases of Texas land by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversary nations.
Voted for SB 8 (2025, regular session), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Voted against Amendment No. 22 to the 2025 budget (SB 1), which directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; the amendment failed 63 to 85.
Voted for the 2026-27 state budget (SB 1) on House passage in April 2025.
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders.
Voted for HB 7 (2025, second called session), allowing civil lawsuits over the manufacture and distribution of abortion-inducing drugs.
In the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker, voted for Dustin Burrows, who was elected Speaker, over David Cook.
In April 2023 voted yes on the motion to table, and no on adoption of, Amendment No. 45 to the budget, which barred state spending on vouchers or similar programs.
Voted against Amendment No. 2 to HB 1 (November 2023), which removed education savings accounts from the bill.
Voted for SB 14 (2023), prohibiting gender transition medical treatments for minors.
Voted for the 2023 motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2127, which limits city and county regulations in fields occupied by state law.
Voted for HR 2377 (May 2023), the articles of impeachment against Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was later acquitted by the Senate.
Voted for SB 3 (fourth called session, 2023), funding border barrier construction and border security operations.
Voted for SB 4 (fourth called session, 2023), creating a state criminal offense for illegal entry from a foreign nation.
Authored HB 29 (2025), on water loss reporting by municipal utilities, and HB 1633 (2025), on groundwater permit criteria; both became law.
Authored HB 119 (2025), requiring lobbyist registration for certain activities on behalf of foreign adversaries, which became law.
Authored HB 1690 (2025), on permits to transfer groundwater out of a conservation district; it was vetoed by the governor.

candidates.name: Cory Liu
candidates.current_role: Judge, 250th District Court (Travis County), appointed by Gov. Greg Abbott in 2025
candidates.background: Cory Liu is an Austin native and a Travis County civil district judge. He holds a B.A. in political science from the University of Chicago and a J.D. from Harvard Law School (2015), where he was editor-in-chief of the Harvard Journal of Law & Public Policy. He clerked for Judge Andrew Oldham of the U.S. Fifth Circuit and Judge Danny Boggs of the U.S. Sixth Circuit, and he was an attorney at Butler Snow LLP in Austin before his appointment. Texasjudges.org also lists prior work in the general counsel's office of the governor, as a Texas Supreme Court law clerk, and in the Texas Solicitor General's Office.

priorities.text: Campaigns on ending discrimination and equal justice under the law, including support for what his site calls a colorblind Constitution.
Highlights a record of defending free speech and religious freedom.
Campaigns on law and order, including support for public safety, crime victims, and military members and veterans.

record.text: Appointed by Gov. Greg Abbott in March 2025 to the 250th District Court in Travis County, for a term running through December 31, 2026.
In an October 2025 order in Becker v. UpEquity Title, criticized Travis County's central docket system for the handling of a nearly two-year-old case, according to The Texas Lawbook.

notes.text: State Bar of Texas 2026 Judicial Poll (3rd Court of Appeals, Chief Justice): Darlene Byrne 536 votes, Liu 146 (about 79 percent to 21 percent). The State Bar poll was a non-scientific survey of participating lawyers taken before the March 2026 primaries.
At the time of his 2025 appointment he was president of the Federalist Society's Austin Lawyers Chapter and a steering committee member for the Texas Review of Law and Politics.
Texasjudges.org lists his nonjudicial experience as the governor's general counsel office, a Texas Supreme Court clerkship, and the Texas Solicitor General's Office.

candidates.name: Darlene Byrne
candidates.current_role: Chief Justice, Third Court of Appeals, since 2021 (elected 2020)
candidates.background: Darlene Byrne was elected chief justice of the Austin-based Third Court of Appeals in 2020. She practiced employment, commercial and governmental litigation for 13 years before taking the bench, and she graduated magna cum laude from the University of Houston Law Center (1987).

priorities.text: Says appeals should be decided promptly so that people's lives do not languish through delayed decision making.
Campaigns on access to justice for all, regardless of wealth, nationality, gender, race or language.
Says a person's day in court should be treated with dignity and respect.
Campaigns on bringing nearly 25 years of trial and appellate judicial experience to grounded, real-world decisions.

record.text: Presided over the 126th District Court in Travis County from 2001 to 2020 and founded the Travis County Family Drug Treatment Court and a Dual Status Youth docket.
Appointed by the Texas Supreme Court in 2008 as the first vice chair of the Texas Children's Commission, serving as a commissioner or judicial advisor until 2024.
Elected chief justice of the Third Court of Appeals in 2020.

candidates.name: Pete Sessions
candidates.current_role: U.S. Representative for Texas' 17th District since 2021
candidates.background: Pete Sessions was born and raised in Waco and lives there with his wife, Karen. He worked as an executive with AT&T before entering politics. He was first elected to the U.S. House in 1996, lost reelection in 2018 and returned to Congress after winning the 17th District in 2020.

photo.credit: Official portrait, U.S. House of Representatives

priorities.text: Calls for freezing federal spending and cutting waste, fraud and abuse to balance the budget.
Stands with President Trump to build the border wall and strengthen immigration laws.
Describes himself as a pro-life conservative who defends gun rights and religious liberty.
Calls for repealing the Affordable Care Act and replacing it with health insurance reforms.
Supports parental involvement in education and opposes curricula he says promote transgender lifestyles.

record.text: Voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1), the 2025 budget reconciliation law that extended tax cuts and reduced projected federal Medicaid spending, on House passage in May 2025 and final passage in July 2025.
Voted for the Laken Riley Act (S. 5), which requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft-related or certain violent crimes, in January 2025.
Voted for the SAVE Act (H.R. 22), which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections, in April 2025.
Voted for the Protect Children's Innocence Act (H.R. 3492), which would make certain gender transition procedures on minors a federal crime, in December 2025.
Voted for the Do No Harm in Medicaid Act (H.R. 498), which would bar Medicaid funding for gender transition procedures for minors, in December 2025.
Voted against H.J.Res. 72, a resolution to end the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods, in February 2026.
Voted against H.R. 1834, which would extend expanded Affordable Care Act premium tax credits for three years and passed the House 230 to 196, in January 2026.
Voted for the Secure America Act (S. 2), which passed the House on a party-line vote, in June 2026.
Voted for the Born-Alive Abortion Survivors Protection Act (H.R. 21) in January 2025.
Introduced the Fraud Prevention and Accountability Act to create a permanent Treasury inspector general focused on fraud in federal awards over $50,000.
Says he was part of the House Republican team that balanced the federal budget four years in a row in the late 1990s.

q_federal_spending.summary: Voted for the 2025 reconciliation law and calls for freezing federal spending to balance the budget.

q_voting_access.summary: Voted for the SAVE Act, which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.

q_trans_minors.summary: Voted for a bill to make certain gender transition procedures on minors a federal crime and for a ban on Medicaid funding for such procedures for minors.

q_tariffs.summary: Voted against ending the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods.

q_abortion.summary: Describes himself as a pro-life conservative and voted for the Born-Alive bill.

q_gun_laws.summary: Says he defends gun rights.

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program; it passed the House 86 to 61.

House sponsor of SB 2 (2025), which created the education savings account program.

candidates.name: Randy Weber
candidates.current_role: U.S. Representative for Texas' 14th District since 2013
candidates.background: Randy Weber founded Weber's Air and Heat, an air conditioning company, in 1981. He attended Alvin Community College and holds a bachelor's degree from the University of Houston at Clear Lake. He served four years in the Texas House before his election to Congress in 2012. He serves on the House Energy and Commerce Committee.

photo.credit: Official portrait, U.S. House of Representatives

priorities.text: Supports lower taxes and opposes wasteful spending.
Supports the oil and gas industry and energy independence.
Supports strict enforcement of immigration laws.
Describes himself as a Christian, conservative, pro-life and Second Amendment supporter.

record.text: Voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1), the 2025 budget reconciliation law that extended tax cuts and reduced projected federal Medicaid spending, on House passage in May 2025 and final passage in July 2025.
Voted for the Laken Riley Act (S. 5), which requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft-related or certain violent crimes, in January 2025.
Voted for the SAVE Act (H.R. 22), which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections, in April 2025.
Voted for the Protect Children's Innocence Act (H.R. 3492), which would make certain gender transition procedures on minors a federal crime, in December 2025.
Voted for the Do No Harm in Medicaid Act (H.R. 498), which would bar Medicaid funding for gender transition procedures for minors, in December 2025.
Voted against H.J.Res. 72, a resolution to end the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods, in February 2026.
Voted against H.R. 1834, which would extend expanded Affordable Care Act premium tax credits for three years and passed the House 230 to 196, in January 2026.
Voted for the Secure America Act (S. 2), which passed the House on a party-line vote, in June 2026.
Voted for the Born-Alive Abortion Survivors Protection Act (H.R. 21) in January 2025.
Authored legislation in the Texas House to combat human trafficking, according to his official biography.

q_federal_spending.summary: Voted for the 2025 reconciliation law, which reduced projected federal Medicaid spending.

q_voting_access.summary: Voted for the SAVE Act, which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.

q_trans_minors.summary: Voted for a bill to make certain gender transition procedures on minors a federal crime and for a ban on Medicaid funding for such procedures for minors.

q_tariffs.summary: Voted against ending the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods.

q_abortion.summary: Describes himself as pro-life and voted for the Born-Alive bill.

q_gun_laws.summary: Opposes gun control measures.

q_fossil_priority.summary: Supports policies that advocate for the oil and gas industry and energy independence.

She was appointed in 2026 to a U.S. Department of Education workforce development commission.

priorities.text: Says parents, not district offices or consultants, should have the first and last word on what children are taught.
Promotes literacy, classical education and the study of the Bible's place in history.
Lists increasing investment in education, restoring values and fighting crime as priorities.
Advocates public, private, charter and home school options.
Has called for removing critical race theory from curriculum and for adopting textbooks that uphold Texas values.

record.text: Supported the 2026 statewide required reading list that includes Bible passages, saying the readings give insight into traditions that shaped Western civilization; the board adopted it 9-4.
During 2026 social studies debates, voted against amendments seeking to expand coverage of race-based slavery and segregation, according to the Texas Tribune.

notes.text: The Houston Chronicle reported in 2022 that she rallied with Trump supporters at the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, and was voted off the Alvin ISD board in 2021 after her participation became known.
In June 2026 Democratic board member Marisa Perez-Diaz sent her a cease-and-desist letter over posts calling Perez-Diaz a Marxist; Pickren described the claims as meritless.
Endorsed by Donald Trump, U.S. Education Secretary Linda McMahon, Ben Carson and Texas Right to Life.
Did not respond to the 2026 League of Women Voters of Texas questionnaire.

q_vouchers.summary: Advocates public, private, charter and home school options and has cited school choice as a solution.

q_ten_commandments.summary: The Texas Tribune reports she sees having God in schools as a solution; she supported Bible passages in the reading list. This is related to, but not the same as, the display requirement.

issue_notes.summary: In 2022 said Texas should do away with STAAR testing because it pushes teaching to the test.
In 2022 said charter schools should be brought to poor areas where public schools are failing and that the board should control all charter approvals.

candidates.name: Kevin Jewell
candidates.current_role: Justice, Fourteenth Court of Appeals, Place 2, since 2017 (elected 2016)
candidates.background: Kevin Jewell is a Houston appellate judge seeking the chief justice seat being vacated by Chief Justice Tracy Christopher. He was elected to Place 2 on the Fourteenth Court of Appeals in 2016 after 23 years in private practice, most recently as a litigation and appellate shareholder at Chamberlain, Hrdlicka, White, Williams & Aughtry, where he chaired the appellate practice group. He has been board certified in civil appellate law since 1998. He holds a B.B.A. from the University of Texas at Austin and a law degree from the University of Houston Law Center (1993).

photo.credit: Official portrait, Fourteenth Court of Appeals (txcourts.gov)

priorities.text: Says he applies the law as written and will never legislate from the bench.
Says a judge's core job is to give all parties a fair day in court, regardless of personal beliefs or partisan affiliation.
Says he wants to ensure the courts never become another political arena.

promises.text: Says he will treat everyone who comes before the Fourteenth Court of Appeals with fairness and dignity.

record.text: Elected to the Fourteenth Court of Appeals, Place 2, in November 2016 and re-elected in 2022.
Before taking the bench, handled hundreds of appeals and argued more than 100 cases in the Supreme Court of Texas, Texas intermediate appellate courts and federal courts of appeals.

notes.text: Houston Chronicle editorial board endorsed Sarah Beth Landau (4.5 stars) and rated Jewell 4 stars, calling him widely respected and noting he received very high ratings in the Houston Bar Association judicial evaluation.
Houston Bar Association 2026 Judicial Preference Poll: Jewell 284 votes, Landau 250. The HBA poll had 769 participating members and is not an HBA endorsement.

State Bar of Texas 2026 Judicial Poll: Landau 522 votes, Jewell 422 (about 55 percent to 45 percent). The State Bar poll was a non-scientific survey of participating lawyers taken before the March 2026 primaries.
Endorsed by the Texas Civil Justice League PAC.
If Jewell wins, the governor will appoint a replacement for his Place 2 seat; if he loses, he keeps Place 2, which has four years remaining, according to the Houston Chronicle.

candidates.current_role: Managing partner, O'Neil Wysocki Family Law (Houston)
candidates.background: Todd Frankfort is a native Houstonian and family lawyer with more than 30 years in private practice. He is board certified in family law and has handled marital property, custody, child support enforcement and family law appeals, after earlier work in real estate and commercial litigation. He holds a B.A. in American studies from the University of Texas at Austin (1990) and a J.D. from South Texas College of Law (1994). He won the Republican nomination after a May 2026 primary runoff.

priorities.text: Campaigns on upholding the Constitution and well-established precedent.
Says he will promote transparency, accessibility and equal treatment under the law to restore public confidence in the courts.
Campaigns on fairness and predictability through consistent application of the law.
Cites public safety and support from law enforcement groups.
Says his family law experience would add expertise that is not well represented on the appellate courts.

promises.text: Says he will review each case under the Constitution, existing law and prior precedent, and states that it is not his job to change the law.

notes.text: Houston Chronicle editorial board endorsed incumbent Veronica Rivas-Molloy (4 stars) and rated Frankfort 3.5 stars, saying his family law experience is relevant to many cases before the court; the board endorsed Frankfort in the Republican primary and runoff.

Houston Bar Association 2026 Judicial Preference Poll: Rivas-Molloy 299 votes, Frankfort 232. The HBA poll had 769 participating members and is not an HBA endorsement.

Valoree Swanson and Charles Cunningham, Harris County Commissioner Tom Ramsey, former Texas Supreme Court Justice Eva Guzman and former Court of Criminal Appeals Judge Michelle Slaughter.
Named a Super Lawyer each year since 2012 and received Houston Bar Association President's Awards in 2004 and 2012, according to his campaign.

q_textualism.summary: Says he favors judicial restraint and strict interpretation of statutes, that judges must apply the law as written, and that changing the law is the legislature's job.

candidates.name: August Pfluger
candidates.current_role: U.S. Representative for Texas' 11th District since 2021
candidates.background: August Pfluger grew up in San Angelo and retired as a colonel after 26 years in the U.S. Air Force, where he flew the F-22 and commanded a squadron. He served as an adviser on the National Security Council under President Trump. He has represented the 11th District since 2021 and serves on the Energy and Commerce and Homeland Security committees. He lives in San Angelo with his wife and three daughters.

photo.credit: Official portrait, U.S. House of Representatives

priorities.text: Campaigns on border security, finishing the wall and strengthening immigration enforcement.
Campaigns on defending the oil and gas industry and energy independence.
Campaigns on locking in the 2025 tax cuts.
Says he defends the Second Amendment and religious liberty.

record.text: Voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1), the 2025 budget reconciliation law that extended tax cuts and reduced projected federal Medicaid spending, on House passage in May 2025 and final passage in July 2025.
Voted for the Laken Riley Act (S. 5), which requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft-related or certain violent crimes, in January 2025.
Voted for the SAVE Act (H.R. 22), which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections, in April 2025.
Voted for the Protect Children's Innocence Act (H.R. 3492), which would make certain gender transition procedures on minors a federal crime, in December 2025.
Voted for the Do No Harm in Medicaid Act (H.R. 498), which would bar Medicaid funding for gender transition procedures for minors, in December 2025.
Voted against H.J.Res. 72, a resolution to end the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods, in February 2026.
Voted against H.R. 1834, which would extend expanded Affordable Care Act premium tax credits for three years and passed the House 230 to 196, in January 2026.
Voted for the Secure America Act (S. 2), which passed the House on a party-line vote, in June 2026.
Voted for the Born-Alive Abortion Survivors Protection Act (H.R. 21) in January 2025.
Sponsored legislation repealing the federal natural gas tax that President Trump signed into law, according to his campaign.
Introduced the Conscience Protection Act of 2025 to protect health care providers who decline to take part in abortions.
Helped author H.R. 2, a 2023 border bill to resume wall construction and add Border Patrol agents.
Voted to object to counting electoral votes from Arizona and/or Pennsylvania on January 6, 2021.

q_federal_spending.summary: Voted for the 2025 reconciliation law, which reduced projected federal Medicaid spending.

q_voting_access.summary: Voted for the SAVE Act, which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.

q_trans_minors.summary: Voted for a bill to make certain gender transition procedures on minors a federal crime and for a ban on Medicaid funding for such procedures for minors.

q_tariffs.summary: Voted against ending the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods.

q_oilgas_rules.summary: Sponsored the repeal of the federal natural gas tax, a fee on methane emissions.

q_fossil_priority.summary: Says he is fighting for total energy independence and supports oil and gas producers.

q_abortion.summary: Says life begins at conception and lists a bill to defend the unborn under any circumstances.

q_gun_laws.summary: Says he is defending the Second Amendment rights of law-abiding citizens.

q_deportation.summary: Cites more than 2 million removals and self-deportations as a promise kept on deporting criminal illegal aliens.

issue_notes.summary: Supports the American Confidence in Elections Act to strengthen voter ID requirements and bar noncitizen voting.
Introduced the RAPID Act to reimburse farmers and ranchers for property damage tied to illegal immigration.

priorities.text: Lists property tax relief, affordability, protecting water resources, investing in education and responsible growth as priorities.
Wants to meet the needs of a growing state while protecting the Hill Country from "incompatible industrial development."

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on its April 2025 House passage vote.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the House school finance and teacher pay bill.
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025), the final version of the school finance bill.
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring display of the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), the constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent felony charges.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned consumable hemp-derived THC products (later vetoed by the governor).
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting purchases of Texas land by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversary nations.
Voted for SB 8 (2025, regular session), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Voted against Amendment No. 22 to the 2025 budget (SB 1), which directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; the amendment failed 63 to 85.
Voted for the 2026-27 state budget (SB 1) on House passage in April 2025.
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders.
Voted for HB 7 (2025, second called session), allowing civil lawsuits over the manufacture and distribution of abortion-inducing drugs.
In the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker, voted for David Cook over Dustin Burrows, who was elected Speaker.

In April 2023 voted absent (statement of vote: intended or would have voted yes) on the motion to table, and no on adoption of, Amendment No. 45 to the budget, which barred state spending on vouchers or similar programs.
Voted against Amendment No. 2 to HB 1 (November 2023), which removed education savings accounts from the bill.
Voted for SB 14 (2023), prohibiting gender transition medical treatments for minors.
Voted for the 2023 motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2127, which limits city and county regulations in fields occupied by state law.

candidates.background: Hoppy Haden is the incumbent Caldwell County Judge. He owns Clear Creek, Inc., a construction, environmental, and farm and ranch services company, and reported more than 30 years in the environmental industry in 2017. record.text: As a commissioner he chaired a host agreement advisory committee on a proposed landfill and worked with TxDOT on funding to widen Highway 21, according to his 2017 candidate profile.

notes.text: Won the March 3, 2026 Republican primary over former County Judge Ken Schawe, 2,122 votes to 1,336.

In July 2026 a local group, the Caldwell Data Center Action Team, called for his resignation and asked the Texas Rangers, the Attorney General's Office, and the district attorney to investigate after he disclosed signing a pre-sale agreement on his land with a company exploring a data center; Haden denied a conflict of interest, said he filed a conflict disclosure and would recuse himself from county matters involving the property, and said he would not resign. No investigation had been reported opened as of that report.
CBS Austin confirmed that a land-buying company owner gave $17,000 to his campaign since February 2026.
Local coverage in December 2025 described the 2026 Republican primary against former Judge Ken Schawe, who served from 2015 to 2018, as competitive.

candidates.name: Eric Flores
candidates.current_role: Attorney and former assistant U.S. attorney
candidates.background: Eric Flores grew up in the Rio Grande Valley and is from Mission. He was commissioned as an Army infantry officer through the Texas Army National Guard after graduating from the University of Texas at Austin and supported Border Patrol operations. He served as an assistant U.S. attorney in the Southern District of Texas and is a partner at a statewide law firm. He won the March 2026 Republican primary over former Rep. Mayra Flores.

priorities.text: Supports energy, agriculture and shipping development in South Texas by opposing federal regulations that slow projects.
Campaigns on lowering the cost of living by limiting federal spending and supporting affordable housing.
Campaigns on federal investment in South Texas water infrastructure and regional water planning.
Campaigns on reducing VA wait times and expanding veterans' health care.
Calls for reducing illegal immigration while making legal immigration efficient for South Texas employers.

promises.text: Says he would oppose taxing or cutting seniors' benefits.

notes.text: Endorsed by President Trump, Gov. Greg Abbott, Speaker Mike Johnson and the National Border Patrol Council.

q_federal_spending.summary: Says he would limit federal spending to curb inflation while opposing cuts to seniors' benefits.

candidates.name: Vicente Gonzalez
candidates.current_role: U.S. Representative for Texas' 34th District since 2023
candidates.background: Vicente Gonzalez earned a GED after leaving high school, then degrees from Del Mar College and a law degree from what is now Texas A&M University School of Law. He founded the law firm V. Gonzalez and Associates. He represented the 15th District from 2017 to 2023 and has represented the 34th since 2023. He serves on the House Financial Services Committee.

priorities.text: Campaigns on protecting seniors' benefits and health care access.
Campaigns on women's rights, including workplace protections and health care access.
Campaigns on education funding and veterans' benefits.
Campaigns on job growth through workforce development and support for local businesses.

record.text: Voted against the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1), the 2025 budget reconciliation law that extended tax cuts and reduced projected federal Medicaid spending, on House passage in May 2025 and final passage in July 2025.
Voted for the Laken Riley Act (S. 5), which requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft-related or certain violent crimes, in January 2025.
Voted against the SAVE Act (H.R. 22), which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections, in April 2025.
Voted for the Protect Children's Innocence Act (H.R. 3492), which would make certain gender transition procedures on minors a federal crime, in December 2025.
Voted for the Do No Harm in Medicaid Act (H.R. 498), which would bar Medicaid funding for gender transition procedures for minors, in December 2025.
Voted for H.J.Res. 72, a resolution to end the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods, in February 2026.
Voted for H.R. 1834, which would extend expanded Affordable Care Act premium tax credits for three years and passed the House 230 to 196, in January 2026.
Voted against the Secure America Act (S. 2), which passed the House on a party-line vote, in June 2026.
Voted against the Department of Homeland Security Appropriations Act, 2026 (H.R. 7744) in March 2026.
Voted to cap insulin costs at $35 a month, according to his campaign.
Secured permits for liquefied natural gas projects at the Port of Brownsville and funding to deepen the ship channel, according to his campaign.
Introduced legislation to forgive up to $25,000 in student loan debt.

notes.text: Endorsed by the Texas AFL-CIO, Texas AFT, the National Education Association and Texas Farm Bureau AGFUND; LUPE Votes endorsed him with conditions.

q_federal_spending.summary: Voted against the 2025 reconciliation law, which reduced projected federal Medicaid spending.

q_voting_access.summary: Voted against the SAVE Act, which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.

q_trans_minors.summary: Voted for a bill to make certain gender transition procedures on minors a federal crime and for a ban on Medicaid funding for such procedures for minors.

q_tariffs.summary: Voted for a resolution to end the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods.

q_legal_status.summary: Proposed the Save the American Workforce Act to let businesses sponsor undocumented immigrants with at least five years in the U.S. and no criminal record for renewable three-year visas; he describes it as "a temporary path," and it would not offer citizenship.

q_deportation.summary: Supports deporting violent criminals but opposes what he calls hyperaggressive ICE raids.

q_abortion.summary: His campaign accomplishments page says he supports "assuring every woman retains the right to make her own healthcare decisions."

issue_notes.summary: Commits to enforcing the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement's labor, intellectual property and free trade standards.

candidates.background: Oscar Longoria is serving his seventh term representing House District 35 in Hidalgo and Cameron counties. In 2025 he chaired the House Permanent Standing Subcommittee on Workforce.

photo.credit: Official portrait, Texas House of Representatives

record.text: Voted against SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on its April 2025 House passage vote.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the House school finance and teacher pay bill.
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025), the final version of the school finance bill.
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring display of the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), the constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent felony charges.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations.
Voted against SB 3 (2025), which would have banned consumable hemp-derived THC products (later vetoed by the governor).
Voted against SB 17 (2025), restricting purchases of Texas land by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversary nations.
Voted for SB 8 (2025, regular session), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Voted for Amendment No. 22 to the 2025 budget (SB 1), which directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; the amendment failed 63 to 85.
Voted for the 2026-27 state budget (SB 1) on House passage in April 2025.
Was absent for the vote on SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders.
Was absent for the vote on HB 7 (2025, second called session), allowing civil lawsuits over the manufacture and distribution of abortion-inducing drugs.
In the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker, voted for Dustin Burrows, who was elected Speaker, over David Cook.
In April 2023 voted no on the motion to table, and yes on adoption of, Amendment No. 45 to the budget, which barred state spending on vouchers or similar programs.
Voted for Amendment No. 2 to HB 1 (November 2023), which removed education savings accounts from the bill.
Voted against SB 14 (2023), prohibiting gender transition medical treatments for minors.
Voted against the 2023 motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2127, which limits city and county regulations in fields occupied by state law.
Voted for HR 2377 (May 2023), the articles of impeachment against Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was later acquitted by the Senate.
Voted for SB 3 (fourth called session, 2023), funding border barrier construction and border security operations.
Voted against SB 4 (fourth called session, 2023), creating a state criminal offense for illegal entry from a foreign nation.
Was recorded present at the August 5, 2025 quorum call, when the House lacked a quorum during the first called session.
Authored HB 1899 (2025), on the age requirement for public fireworks display permits, which became law, and HB 4410 (2025), on Medicaid ambulance reimbursement rates.

Voted against HB 4 (2025 second called session), redrawing Texas congressional districts; it passed 88 to 52.
Voted for a 2023 budget amendment (Amendment No. 45 to HB 1) barring the use of state funds for school vouchers or similar programs; it was adopted 86 to 52.
Voted for the November 2023 amendment offered by Rep. John Raney, Rep. Drew Darby and others that struck the education savings account program from HB 1; it was adopted 84 to 63.
Voted against SB 14 (2023), banning gender transition medical treatments for minors; it passed 87 to 56.
Voted for HR 2377 (2023), impeaching Attorney General Ken Paxton; it was adopted 121 to 23.
Voted against SB 3 (2023 fourth called session), funding state border barrier construction; it passed 84 to 59.
Voted against SB 4 (2023 fourth called session), creating a state offense for illegal entry from a foreign nation; it passed 83 to 61.
Authored HB 3680 (2025) on subdivision plat requirements in certain counties, which became law.

Authored 2025 bills on federal firearm reporting for people recently released from emergency detention (HB 2161) and on local authority to regulate firearms in certain libraries (HB 1138); neither advanced past committee.
Authored HB 5520 (2025) on border protection and economic development programs, which passed the House.

notes.text: Endorsed by the Texas AFL-CIO COPE for the 2026 general election.

q_vouchers.summary: Voted against SB 2, the 2025 education savings account law, and voted for 2023 amendments that blocked voucher or education savings account funding.

q_school_funding.summary: Voted for HB 2, the 2025 school finance bill.

q_ten_commandments.summary: Voted against SB 10 (2025), requiring classroom Ten Commandments displays.

q_medicaid.summary: Voted for a 2025 budget amendment directing the state to seek a waiver to expand Medicaid.

q_bail.summary: Voted for SJR 5 and for SB 9, the 2025 bail measures.

q_cannabis.summary: Voted against SB 3 (2025), which would have banned most hemp-derived THC products.

q_foreign_land.summary: Voted against SB 17 (2025), restricting land purchases tied to designated foreign adversaries.

q_abortion.summary: Voted against SB 33 (2025), a measure restricting abortion access.

q_gun_laws.summary: Voted against SB 1362 (2025) and authored 2025 bills on federal firearm reporting after emergency detention and on local regulation of firearms in libraries.

q_deportation.summary: Voted against SB 8 (2025), requiring sheriff agreements with ICE; voted against SB 4 (2023), creating a state illegal entry offense. No direct statement on deportation priorities was found.

q_border_state.summary: Voted against SB 3 (2023), which funded state border barrier construction.

q_trans_minors.summary: Voted against SB 14 (2023), the ban on gender transition treatments for minors.

He holds a political science degree from Texas A&M University and a law degree from South Texas College of Law, and won a May 2, 2026 special election for this seat.

priorities.text: Calls public safety the first responsibility of government and supports holding violent and repeat offenders accountable.
Says Texas must continue decisive action to secure the border and disrupt criminal networks.
Wants to reduce children's exposure to harmful online content, citing Australia's approach.
Supports limiting appraisal increases, transparency from taxing entities and reducing reliance on property taxes.
Calls for sustained flood mitigation investment in East Montgomery County and the Lake Houston area.

record.text: As district attorney, created an Internet Crimes Against Children division, a public corruption unit and one of the state's early veterans treatment courts.

notes.text: Endorsed by Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, former Sen. Brandon Creighton, law enforcement groups including the Houston Police Officers' Union, and the Texas Trial Lawyers Association PAC.
The Legislature has not met since he took office, so he has no Senate voting record.
No response to the 2026 ATPE candidate survey was posted on the candidate's Teach the Vote page.

q_border_state.summary: Says Texas must continue decisive action to secure the border and support law enforcement efforts.

q_prop_tax_eliminate.summary: Supports reducing reliance on property taxes altogether.

issue_notes.summary: Supports steps to limit minors' exposure to dangerous online content.
Supports comprehensive watershed-wide flood mitigation planning.

candidates.name: Terri Leo Wilson
candidates.current_role: Texas State Representative, District 23, since 2023
candidates.background: Terri Leo Wilson has represented House District 23 since 2023. She is a former special education teacher, case manager and department administrator with degrees from Texas A&M University-Commerce.

photo.credit: Official portrait, Texas House of Representatives

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on its April 2025 House passage vote.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the House school finance and teacher pay bill.
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025), the final version of the school finance bill.
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring display of the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), the constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent felony charges.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned consumable hemp-derived THC products (later vetoed by the governor).
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting purchases of Texas land by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversary nations.
Voted for SB 8 (2025, regular session), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Voted against Amendment No. 22 to the 2025 budget (SB 1), which directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; the amendment failed 63 to 85.
Voted for the 2026-27 state budget (SB 1) on House passage in April 2025.
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders.
Voted for HB 7 (2025, second called session), allowing civil lawsuits over the manufacture and distribution of abortion-inducing drugs.
In the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker, voted for David Cook over Dustin Burrows, who was elected Speaker.
In April 2023 voted yes on the motion to table, and no on adoption of, Amendment No. 45 to the budget, which barred state spending on vouchers or similar programs.
Voted against Amendment No. 2 to HB 1 (November 2023), which removed education savings accounts from the bill.
Voted for SB 14 (2023), prohibiting gender transition medical treatments for minors.
Voted for the 2023 motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2127, which limits city and county regulations in fields occupied by state law.
Voted against HR 2377 (May 2023), the articles of impeachment against Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was later acquitted by the Senate.
Voted for SB 3 (fourth called session, 2023), funding border barrier construction and border security operations.
Voted for SB 4 (fourth called session, 2023), creating a state criminal offense for illegal entry from a foreign nation.
Authored HB 100 (2025), on purchase and use of instructional materials by public schools, which became law.

Authored HB 1485 (2025), to repeal or limit certain taxes including school maintenance and operations property taxes, and HB 518 (2025), on agricultural land ownership by nonresident aliens and foreign entities; neither passed.
Authored HB 4957 and HJR 103 (2025), giving the attorney general authority to prosecute election law offenses; neither passed.

candidates.name: Carrie Isaac
candidates.current_role: State Representative, Texas House District 73, since 2023
candidates.background: Isaac represents Comal County and western Hays County. She ran unsuccessfully for House District 45 in 2020, was first elected to District 73 in 2022 and ran unopposed in the 2026 Republican primary. She is married to former Rep. Jason Isaac.

photo.credit: Official portrait, Texas House of Representatives

priorities.text: Says property taxes are the top issue she hears from voters.
Says unmanaged growth is straining Hill Country water.
Says school funding should follow the student, reward results and support neighborhood schools and parental choice.
Pledges to cut taxes, give communities local control and uphold the rule of law.

promises.text: Says she will seek a 3 percent cap on homestead appraisals, a two-thirds voter approval requirement for tax increases and state spending limits for local governments.
Says she will refile HB 5325, requiring new plats that rely on groundwater to prove an adequate supply.
Says she will help pass legislation setting parameters for data centers and ending tax breaks that subsidize them.

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program; it passed the House 86 to 61.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the main public school finance bill, on third reading; it passed 142 to 5.
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025 school finance); it prevailed 122 to 13.
Voted against a 2025 budget amendment by Rep. John Bucy directing the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; it failed 63 to 85.
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting land purchases by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversary countries; it passed 86 to 59.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), a constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent offenses; it was adopted 133 to 8.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations; it passed 118 to 25.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned most consumable hemp-derived THC products, on second reading; it advanced 95 to 44.
Voted for SB 33 (2025), barring local governments from funding travel for abortion services; it passed 87 to 58.
Voted for SB 8 (2025), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement; it passed 86 to 47.
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms; it passed 82 to 46.
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting the recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders; it passed 86 to 53.
Voted for the conference report on SB 1, the 2026-2027 state budget; it was adopted 107 to 21.
Voted for HB 4 (2025 second called session), redrawing Texas congressional districts; it passed 88 to 52.
Voted for HB 7 (2025 second called session), restricting abortion-inducing drugs; it passed 82 to 48.
Voted against a 2023 budget amendment (Amendment No. 45 to HB 1) barring the use of state funds for school vouchers or similar programs; it was adopted 86 to 52.
Voted against the November 2023 amendment offered by Rep. John Raney, Rep. Drew Darby and others that struck the education savings account program from HB 1; it was adopted 84 to 63.
Voted for SB 14 (2023), banning gender transition medical treatments for minors; it passed 87 to 56.
Voted against HR 2377 (2023), impeaching Attorney General Ken Paxton; it was adopted 121 to 23.
Voted for SB 3 (2023 fourth called session), funding state border barrier construction; it passed 84 to 59.
Voted for SB 4 (2023 fourth called session), creating a state offense for illegal entry from a foreign nation; it passed 83 to 61.
Authored HB 5325 (2025) on groundwater supply evidence for subdivision plats, which did not pass, and HB 218 on directing surplus revenue to a fund for reducing school property taxes.
Authored HB 1337 (2025) on recognition of out-of-state handgun licenses and HB 2882 on the definition of short-barrel firearm.

notes.text: Endorsed in the 2024 Republican primary by Gov. Greg Abbott, who backed incumbents who supported his 2023 education savings account bill, according to ATPE.

candidates.name: Shelby Slawson
candidates.current_role: State Representative, Texas House District 59, since 2021; vice chair of the House Republican Caucus
candidates.background: Slawson represents a north central Texas district that includes Coryell County. She defeated then-Rep. J.D. Sheffield in a July 2020 Republican runoff. Her campaign says she serves as vice chair of the House Republican Caucus and has served on State Affairs, Calendars and Appropriations. She ran unopposed in the 2026 Republican primary.

photo.credit: Official portrait, Texas House of Representatives

priorities.text: Campaign highlights property tax relief, border security investments, Second Amendment rights and parental rights in education.

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program; it passed the House 86 to 61.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the main public school finance bill, on third reading; it passed 142 to 5.
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025 school finance); it prevailed 122 to 13.
Voted against a 2025 budget amendment by Rep. John Bucy directing the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; it failed 63 to 85.
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting land purchases by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversary countries; it passed 86 to 59.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), a constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent offenses; it was adopted 133 to 8.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations; it passed 118 to 25.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned most consumable hemp-derived THC products, on second reading; it advanced 95 to 44.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), the hemp-derived THC products bill, on third reading; it passed 87 to 54.
Voted for SB 33 (2025), barring local governments from funding travel for abortion services; it passed 87 to 58.
Voted for SB 8 (2025), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement; it passed 86 to 47.
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms; it passed 82 to 46.
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting the recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders; it passed 86 to 53.
Voted for the conference report on SB 1, the 2026-2027 state budget; it was adopted 107 to 21.
Voted for HB 4 (2025 second called session), redrawing Texas congressional districts; it passed 88 to 52.
Voted for HB 7 (2025 second called session), restricting abortion-inducing drugs; it passed 82 to 48.
Was recorded present, not voting on a 2023 budget amendment (Amendment No. 45 to HB 1) barring the use of state funds for school vouchers or similar programs; it was adopted 86 to 52.
Voted against the November 2023 amendment offered by Rep. John Raney, Rep. Drew Darby and others that struck the education savings account program from HB 1; it was adopted 84 to 63.
Voted for SB 14 (2023), banning gender transition medical treatments for minors; it passed 87 to 56.
Voted against HR 2377 (2023), impeaching Attorney General Ken Paxton; it was adopted 121 to 23.
Voted for SB 3 (2023 fourth called session), funding state border barrier construction; it passed 84 to 59.
Voted for SB 4 (2023 fourth called session), creating a state offense for illegal entry from a foreign nation; it passed 83 to 61.
Carried the Texas Heartbeat Act (SB 8, 2021) in the House as a first-term member, according to her campaign.
Authored HB 1088 (2025) on the statute of limitations for health care liability claims involving certain gender modification drugs and procedures; it was reported from committee.
Authored HB 3924 (2025) on open carry of a handgun by a uniformed school marshal.

notes.text: Endorsed in the 2024 Republican primary by Gov. Greg Abbott, who backed incumbents who supported his 2023 education savings account bill, according to ATPE.
Her campaign cites Rice University rankings placing her ninth most conservative of 150 House members in 2025.

q_vouchers.summary: Voted for SB 2, the 2025 education savings account law, and voted against 2023 amendments that blocked voucher or education savings account funding.

q_school_funding.summary: Voted for HB 2, the 2025 school finance bill.

q_ten_commandments.summary: Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring classroom Ten Commandments displays.

q_medicaid.summary: Voted against a 2025 budget amendment directing the state to seek a waiver to expand Medicaid.

q_bail.summary: Voted for SJR 5 and for SB 9, the 2025 bail measures.

q_cannabis.summary: Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned most hemp-derived THC products.

q_foreign_land.summary: Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting land purchases tied to designated foreign adversaries.

q_abortion.summary: Carried the 2021 Texas Heartbeat Act in the House and voted for SB 33 and HB 7 in 2025.

q_gun_laws.summary: Voted for SB 1362 (2025), which bars enforcement of extreme risk protective orders.

q_deportation.summary: Voted for SB 8 (2025), requiring sheriff agreements with ICE; voted for SB 4 (2023), creating a state illegal entry offense. No direct statement on deportation priorities was found.

q_border_state.summary: Voted for SB 3 (2023), which funded state border barrier construction.

q_trans_minors.summary: Voted for SB 14 (2023) and authored a 2025 bill on liability claims involving gender modification drugs and procedures.

candidates.name: Lance Gooden
candidates.current_role: U.S. Representative for Texas' 5th District since 2019
candidates.background: Lance Gooden worked in the insurance industry and served three terms in the Texas House. He was first elected to Congress in 2018. He lives with his wife, Alexa, and their two children.

photo.credit: Official portrait, U.S. House of Representatives (Office of the Clerk)

priorities.text: Supports free-market health care solutions to reduce costs and increase patient choice.
Opposes using taxpayer dollars to fund abortion.
Introduced the End Sanctuary Cities Act to penalize officials who interfere with federal immigration enforcement.

record.text: Voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1), the 2025 budget reconciliation law that extended tax cuts and reduced projected federal Medicaid spending, on House passage in May 2025 and final passage in July 2025.
Voted for the Laken Riley Act (S. 5), which requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft-related or certain violent crimes, in January 2025.
Voted for the SAVE Act (H.R. 22), which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections, in April 2025.
Voted for the Protect Children's Innocence Act (H.R. 3492), which would make certain gender transition procedures on minors a federal crime, in December 2025.
Voted for the Do No Harm in Medicaid Act (H.R. 498), which would bar Medicaid funding for gender transition procedures for minors, in December 2025.
Voted against H.J.Res. 72, a resolution to end the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods, in February 2026.
Voted against H.R. 1834, which would extend expanded Affordable Care Act premium tax credits for three years and passed the House 230 to 196, in January 2026.
Voted for the Secure America Act (S. 2), which passed the House on a party-line vote, in June 2026.
Voted for the Born-Alive Abortion Survivors Protection Act (H.R. 21) in January 2025.
Voted against H.R. 8, a 2021 bill to expand background checks on gun sales, citing Second Amendment concerns.
Introduced legislation to bar the federal government from requiring elementary schools to teach gender identity and sex education.
Voted against certifying Arizona and Pennsylvania electoral votes on January 6, 2021.

q_federal_spending.summary: Voted for the 2025 reconciliation law, which reduced projected federal Medicaid spending.

q_voting_access.summary: Voted for the SAVE Act, which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.

q_trans_minors.summary: Voted for a bill to make certain gender transition procedures on minors a federal crime and for a ban on Medicaid funding for such procedures for minors.

q_tariffs.summary: Voted against ending the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods.

q_gun_laws.summary: Voted against H.R. 8, the Bipartisan Background Checks Act of 2021, on March 11, 2021 (roll call 75); the stated reason in the Branch summary was not verified.

q_abortion.summary: Opposes taxpayer funding of abortion and voted for the Born-Alive bill.

candidates.name: Jordan Scott Hoffnagle
candidates.current_role: Republican nominee, Texas House District 100
candidates.background: Hoffnagle describes himself as a Dallas resident who installs equipment for a living and coaches youth sports in the district. He ran unopposed in the 2026 Republican primary and says he is not a career politician.

priorities.text: Proposes locking residential property taxes to the purchase price for as long as the owner holds the property.
Proposes equal custody as the default starting point for two fit parents in family court.
Proposes requiring high schools to accept work-study credit in licensed trades.
Proposes banning automated license plate readers and other mass surveillance without a warrant.
Supports right-to-repair rules and limits on manufacturers disabling purchased products.

promises.text: Says he has drafted a Family Court and Probate Accountability Act, an Attorney Accountability and Client Protection Act, and a Body Worn Camera Transparency Act.
Supports term limits for every political office in Texas.

notes.text: Responded to the 2026 ATPE candidate survey.

q_vouchers.summary: Supports education savings accounts for homeschooling parents, in addition to fully funding public schools.

q_school_funding.summary: Told ATPE district funding should be reviewed case by case and he would not grant blanket funding, while supporting teacher pay raises.

q_medicaid.summary: Supports expanding Medicaid while the federal match stays at or above 90 percent, with an automatic reversal trigger.

q_cannabis.summary: Supports repealing state THC scheduling that drives arrests, Texas-grown cultivation, and expanding the Compassionate Use Program.

issue_notes.summary: Opposes casinos in Dallas and school funding built on gambling, while calling for clarity on fantasy sports and prediction markets.
Supports expanding nuclear energy and continued use of Texas natural gas.
Proposes data center corridors away from neighborhoods, with facilities generating their own power and securing their own water.

candidates.background: Jones represents House District 100 in Dallas, where he was born and raised, and was first elected in 2022. Voted for the November 2023 amendment removing the education savings account program from HB 1 (adopted 84 to 63).

candidates.name: Aicha Davis
candidates.current_role: State Representative, Texas House District 109, since 2025
candidates.background: Davis represents House District 109 in Dallas County and was first elected in 2024. She previously served on the State Board of Education for District 13 from 2019 to 2024. The Texas Tribune lists her occupation as education.

photo.credit: Official portrait, Texas House of Representatives

record.text: Voted against SB 2 (2025), which created a $1 billion education savings account program for private school and homeschool costs; it passed the House 86 to 61.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the school finance and teacher pay bill, on House passage (142 to 5).
Voted for Amendment No. 22 to the 2026-2027 budget (April 2025), which would have directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; it failed 63 to 85.
Voted against SB 17 (2025), restricting land purchases by people and entities tied to designated foreign adversary countries; it passed 86 to 59.
Was recorded absent for the vote on SJR 5 (2025), a proposed constitutional amendment expanding when bail can be denied for certain violent or sexual offenses (adopted 133 to 8).
Voted against SB 9 (2025), changing bail and pretrial release procedures (passed 118 to 25).
Voted against SB 3 (2025), which would have banned most consumable hemp-derived THC products; it passed the House 87 to 54.
Voted against SB 8 (2025), requiring agreements between county sheriffs and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to enforce federal immigration law (passed 86 to 47).
Voted against SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms (passed 82 to 46).
Voted against SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders (passed 86 to 53).

Was not recorded voting on the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HJR 7 (2025), a constitutional amendment dedicating sales tax revenue to the Texas water fund (122 to 12), and stated in the journal that she would have voted yes.
Voted for SB 7 (2025), on water infrastructure financing (passed 136 to 0).
Voted against SB 33 (2025), barring local governments from funding travel for abortions (passed 87 to 58).
Was recorded absent for the vote on HB 4 (2025, second called session), redrawing Texas congressional districts (passed 88 to 52).
Was recorded absent for the vote on HB 7 (2025, second called session), prohibiting the manufacture and provision of abortion-inducing drugs and authorizing private lawsuits (passed 82 to 48).
Authored HB 4129 (2025), on contracts between the Department of Family and Protective Services and single source continuum contractors, which became law.
Authored HB 5516 (2025), on applications for new charter school campuses.

notes.text: Endorsed by Texas Parent PAC in the 2024 Democratic primary, according to ATPE.
Endorsed by the Texas AFL-CIO COPE for the 2026 general election.

candidates.name: Toni Rose
candidates.current_role: State Representative, Texas House District 110, since 2013
candidates.background: Rose represents District 110, which includes Oak Cliff, Pleasant Grove and Balch Springs in Dallas County. She is an alumna of Paul Quinn College and previously served on City of Dallas boards, including the Planning and Zoning Commission. In the 89th Legislature she was vice chair of the House Calendars Committee and served on Appropriations and Human Services, according to her official biography.

priorities.text: Says her legislative focus is mental health, access to affordable health care and criminal justice reform.
Highlights state budget funding she secured for mental health authorities, early childhood intervention and school meal programs.

record.text: Authored HB 12, which extended postpartum Medicaid coverage for new mothers from two to 12 months, according to her official biography.

In 2025 authored HB 2402 (Medicaid fees and rates), HB 2809 (DFPS reporting on youth suicide attempts), HB 5155 (maternal opioid misuse model under Medicaid) and HB 5394, which became law, and HB 2777 to bar the death penalty for people with severe mental illness, which failed in committee.
Voted against SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on third reading.
In 2023 voted for the April 2023 budget amendment barring state funds for vouchers and for the November 2023 amendment removing education savings accounts from HB 1.
Voted for HB 2 (2025 school finance) on third reading and voted to concur in the final Senate version.
Voted for a 2025 budget amendment (Amendment No. 22 to SB 1) directing the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid, which failed 63 to 85.
Voted against SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms.
Voted for SJR 5 (the 2025 bail constitutional amendment) and voted against SB 9 (2025 bail procedures).
Voted against SB 3 (2025), which would have banned most hemp-derived THC products, on third reading.
In 2025 voted against SB 8 (requiring certain sheriffs to enter agreements with ICE) and SB 1362 (barring enforcement of extreme risk protective orders).
In the August 2025 second special session voted against HB 4 (2025 mid-decade congressional redistricting) and against HB 7 (2025, civil lawsuits over abortion-inducing drugs).

In 2023 voted against SB 14 (ban on gender transition treatments for minors), HB 2127 (state preemption of local regulations), SB 3 (state border barrier funding) and SB 4 (state illegal entry offense).
Voted for impeaching Attorney General Ken Paxton in May 2023.
Voted for Dustin Burrows over David Cook in the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker of the House.
Was recorded absent on August 5, 2025, when the House lacked a quorum during the House Democrats' walkout over congressional redistricting.

notes.text: Ran unopposed in the 2026 Democratic primary; no other candidate is listed for this seat in this guide's roster.

candidates.name: John Bryant
candidates.current_role: State Representative, Texas House District 114, since 2023
candidates.background: Bryant served in the Texas House from 1974 to 1983 and was elected to the U.S. House in 1983, and he ran for the U.S. Senate in 1996, according to ATPE. He returned to the Texas House after winning District 114 in 2022. His campaign says Texas Monthly named him one of its Ten Best Legislators three times.

photo.credit: Official portrait, Texas House of Representatives

priorities.text: Says he is running because the threat to democracy requires everyone to get off the sidelines.

record.text: In 2025 authored HB 1355 (Medicaid expansion), HB 2570 (extreme risk protective orders), HB 3247 (electronic voter registration), HB 5163 and HB 5598 (minimum wage and living wage study) and HB 5156 (TRS cost-of-living adjustments); none became law.
Voted against SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on third reading.
In 2023 voted for the April 2023 budget amendment barring state funds for vouchers and for the November 2023 amendment removing education savings accounts from HB 1.
Voted for HB 2 (2025 school finance) on third reading and voted to concur in the final Senate version.
Voted for a 2025 budget amendment (Amendment No. 22 to SB 1) directing the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid, which failed 63 to 85.
Voted against SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms.
Voted for SJR 5 (the 2025 bail constitutional amendment) and voted against SB 9 (2025 bail procedures).
Voted against SB 3 (2025), which would have banned most hemp-derived THC products, on third reading.

In 2025 voted against SB 17 (land purchases tied to designated foreign adversaries), SB 8 (requiring certain sheriffs to enter agreements with ICE) and SB 1362 (barring enforcement of extreme risk protective orders).
In the August 2025 second special session voted against HB 4 (2025 mid-decade congressional redistricting) and against HB 7 (2025, civil lawsuits over abortion-inducing drugs).

In 2023 voted against SB 14 (ban on gender transition treatments for minors), HB 2127 (state preemption of local regulations), SB 3 (state border barrier funding) and SB 4 (state illegal entry offense).
Voted for impeaching Attorney General Ken Paxton in May 2023.
Was recorded absent on August 5, 2025, when the House lacked a quorum during the House Democrats' walkout over congressional redistricting.

notes.text: Was recorded present but not voting in the January 2025 Speaker runoff.
Endorsed by Texas Parent PAC in 2022, according to ATPE.

q_gun_laws.summary: Authored HB 2570 (2025) on extreme risk protective orders and voted against SB 1362.
