candidates.current_role: State Representative, Texas House District 64, since 2025
candidates.background: Hopper is a software engineer and a chief warrant officer in the Texas State Guard. He lost a 2022 bid for the seat and won it in 2024 after a Republican primary runoff. He won the 2026 Republican primary.

priorities.text: Lists eliminating property taxes as a top priority.

candidates.name: Jared Patterson
candidates.current_role: State Representative, Texas House District 106, since 2019
candidates.background: Patterson, a Texas A&M University graduate, was first elected in 2018 to represent north central and eastern Denton County. His House biography describes him as a full-spectrum conservative and highlights his role in passing constitutional carry, the Texas Heartbeat Act, and the 2023 READER Act on school library materials.

photo.credit: Official portrait, Texas House of Representatives

priorities.text: Says he co-authored HB 2 (2025), which he says added $8.5 billion for public education.
Says he co-authored SB 2 (2025), creating education savings accounts, and SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays.
Cites votes to raise border security funding and support for SB 8 (2025) on 287(g) agreements.
Cites election measures including SJR 37 (2025) on citizenship to vote and SB 1 (2021).

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created a $1 billion education savings account program for private school and homeschool costs; it passed the House 86 to 61.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the school finance and teacher pay bill, on House passage (142 to 5).
Voted against Amendment No. 22 to the 2026-2027 budget (April 2025), which would have directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; it failed 63 to 85.
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting land purchases by people and entities tied to designated foreign adversary countries; it passed 86 to 59.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), a proposed constitutional amendment expanding when bail can be denied for certain violent or sexual offenses (adopted 133 to 8).
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail and pretrial release procedures (passed 118 to 25).
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned most consumable hemp-derived THC products; it passed the House 87 to 54.
Voted for SB 8 (2025), requiring agreements between county sheriffs and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to enforce federal immigration law (passed 86 to 47).
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms (passed 82 to 46).
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders (passed 86 to 53).
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HJR 7 (2025), a constitutional amendment dedicating sales tax revenue to the Texas water fund (122 to 12).
Voted for SB 33 (2025), barring local governments from funding travel for abortions (passed 87 to 58).
Voted for HB 4 (2025, second called session), redrawing Texas congressional districts (passed 88 to 52).
Voted for HB 7 (2025, second called session), prohibiting the manufacture and provision of abortion-inducing drugs and authorizing private lawsuits (passed 82 to 48).
Voted for SB 14 (2023), banning gender transition medical treatments for minors (passed 87 to 56).
Voted for the May 2023 resolution impeaching Attorney General Ken Paxton (adopted 121 to 23).
Voted against Amendment No. 45 to the 2023 House budget, barring state money for vouchers or education savings accounts (adopted 86 to 52).
Voted against the November 2023 amendment removing the education savings account program from HB 1 (adopted 84 to 63).
Voted for SB 3 (2023, fourth called session), funding border barrier construction and border security operations (passed 84 to 59).
Voted for SB 4 (2023, fourth called session), creating a state offense for illegal entry (passed 83 to 61).
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2127 (2023), which preempts certain city and county regulation (84 to 58).
Authored HB 4353 (2025), requiring voter approval of wind, solar, or energy storage projects in certain counties, and HB 3244 (2025) on wind turbine siting; both were referred to committee.
Authored HB 621 (2025), limiting property owners' association restrictions on political speech, and HB 2890 (2025), on an interstate liquefied natural gas compact; both became law.

notes.text: Endorsed by Gov. Greg Abbott in the 2024 Republican primary and by the Texas Home School Coalition in 2022, according to ATPE.
Did not respond to the 2018 through 2026 ATPE candidate surveys.

candidates.name: Brian Walker
candidates.current_role: Justice, Second Court of Appeals, Place 7
candidates.background: Brian Walker is a native Texan and a justice on the Fort Worth-based Second Court of Appeals. After law school at the University of Houston (J.D. 2003), he was a prosecutor in the Harrison County District Attorney's Office for nearly two years and then spent almost 15 years in private practice handling military and veterans law, civil litigation and criminal defense, trying more than 75 jury trials. He served nine years as a Judge Advocate in the U.S. Air Force Reserves. He also holds a B.S. from Texas State University, an M.A. in international relations from the University of Oklahoma and a master's degree from Dallas Theological Seminary.

record.text: Authored about 100 civil and criminal appellate briefs while in private practice and co-founded a Tarrant County program providing pro bono legal services to veterans.

notes.text: Texasjudges.org lists no opponent in the November 2026 general election.
Named a Super Lawyer in 2020 and 2021 and a Lawyer on the Rise by Texas Lawyer magazine in 2016, according to his official biography.

candidates.name: Andy Eads
candidates.current_role: Denton County Judge since 2019
candidates.background: Andy Eads is a fifth-generation Denton County resident who served on the Denton County Commissioners Court before becoming county judge in 2019. He holds a bachelor's degree in business administration from Howard Payne University and a master's in public administration from the University of North Texas. He lives in Flower Mound.

priorities.text: Campaigns on keeping property taxes low, strengthening public safety, improving transportation infrastructure, and promoting economic development.
Says managing rapid growth in a county of more than one million residents is the county's biggest challenge.
Says he will plan ahead and work with cities, regional partners and state leaders, and keep county government from growing faster than needed.
Says he wants to keep property taxes low through the senior tax freeze and homestead exemption.

promises.text: Says he will partner with the Texas Department of Transportation on state highway, farm-to-market road and interstate projects in the county.

record.text: Championed two countywide road bond elections and credits himself with work on SH 114, US 380 reconstruction, the I-635 agreement and the 35Express project.

The FY2027 recommended county budget presented to the Commissioners Court in August 2026 was about $494.5 million with a tax rate of $0.183394 per $100, described by the budget office as the lowest since at least 1986 and a 1.4% decrease from FY2026.
The FY2027 recommended budget keeps a homestead exemption (1% of value, minimum $5,000) for a seventh year and the senior and disabled homestead tax ceiling for an eighth year.

notes.text: Faces Democrat Nick Pappas in the November 3, 2026 general election.

q_county_tax.summary: Lists keeping property taxes low and disciplined spending among his top priorities, while also prioritizing road investment.

issue_notes.summary: Emphasizes partnerships with TxDOT and regional agencies on highway and road projects.

candidates.name: Brian Harrison
candidates.current_role: Texas State Representative, District 10
candidates.background: Brian Harrison represents House District 10, which covers all of Ellis County. During the Trump administration he served as chief of staff at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. He is a graduate of Ovilla Christian School.

photo.credit: Official portrait, Texas House of Representatives

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on its April 2025 House passage vote.
Voted against HB 2 (2025), the House school finance and teacher pay bill.
Voted against the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025), the final version of the school finance bill.
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring display of the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), the constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent felony charges.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations.
Voted against SB 3 (2025), which would have banned consumable hemp-derived THC products (later vetoed by the governor).
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting purchases of Texas land by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversary nations.
Voted for SB 8 (2025, regular session), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Voted against Amendment No. 22 to the 2025 budget (SB 1), which directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; the amendment failed 63 to 85.
Voted against the 2026-27 state budget (SB 1) on House passage in April 2025.
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders.

Voted against HB 7 (2025, second called session), allowing civil lawsuits over the manufacture and distribution of abortion-inducing drugs; a statement of vote in the journal says the member intended to vote yes.
In the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker, voted for David Cook over Dustin Burrows, who was elected Speaker.
In April 2023 voted yes on the motion to table, and no on adoption of, Amendment No. 45 to the budget, which barred state spending on vouchers or similar programs.
Voted against Amendment No. 2 to HB 1 (November 2023), which removed education savings accounts from the bill.
Voted for SB 14 (2023), prohibiting gender transition medical treatments for minors.
Voted for the 2023 motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2127, which limits city and county regulations in fields occupied by state law.
Voted against HR 2377 (May 2023), the articles of impeachment against Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was later acquitted by the Senate.
Voted for SB 3 (fourth called session, 2023), funding border barrier construction and border security operations.
Voted for SB 4 (fourth called session, 2023), creating a state criminal offense for illegal entry from a foreign nation.
Voted against SB 31 (2025), which clarified medical exceptions to the state abortion ban; it passed 134 to 4. In floor remarks he said it was irresponsible to change the state's pro-life protections.
Authored HB 698 and HJR 64 (2025) to abolish property taxes; neither advanced past committee.
Authored HB 847 (2025), prohibiting public funding for gender reassignment, and HB 2691 (2025), barring lobbyist expenditures and gifts to public servants; neither became law.

q_vouchers.summary: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program.

q_school_funding.summary: Voted against HB 2 (2025), the school finance and teacher pay bill.

q_ten_commandments.summary: Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays in classrooms.

q_medicaid.summary: Voted against a 2025 budget amendment directing the state to seek a waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility.

q_bail.summary: Voted for SJR 5 and SB 9 (2025), which expand denial of bail and tighten bail procedures for violent felony charges.

q_foreign_land.summary: Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting land purchases by people and entities tied to foreign adversary nations.

q_deportation.summary: Voted for SB 8 (2025), requiring certain sheriffs to seek immigration enforcement agreements with ICE.

q_gun_laws.summary: Voted for SB 1362 (2025), which bars recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective (red flag) orders.

q_abortion.summary: Voted for HB 7 (2025), allowing civil suits over the distribution of abortion-inducing drugs (per a journal statement of vote).

q_trans_minors.summary: Voted for SB 14 (2023), which prohibits gender transition medical treatments for minors.

q_preemption.summary: Voted for final passage of HB 2127 (2023), which limits local regulations in fields occupied by state law.

q_border_state.summary: Voted for SB 3 (2023, fourth called session), funding state border barrier construction and border operations.

q_prop_tax_eliminate.summary: Authored HB 698 and HJR 64 (2025) to abolish property taxes.

q_ethics.summary: Authored HB 2691 (2025) to prohibit certain lobbyist expenditures and gifts to public servants.

record.text: Voted against the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1), the 2025 budget reconciliation law that extended tax cuts and reduced projected federal Medicaid spending, on House passage in May 2025 and final passage in July 2025.

Voted against the SAVE Act (H.R. 22), which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections, in April 2025.
Voted against the Protect Children's Innocence Act (H.R. 3492), which would make certain gender transition procedures on minors a federal crime, in December 2025.
Voted against the Do No Harm in Medicaid Act (H.R. 498), which would bar Medicaid funding for gender transition procedures for minors, in December 2025.
Voted for H.J.Res. 72, a resolution to end the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods, in February 2026.
Voted for H.R. 1834, which would extend expanded Affordable Care Act premium tax credits for three years and passed the House 230 to 196, in January 2026.
Voted against the Secure America Act (S. 2), which passed the House on a party-line vote, in June 2026.
Led the introduction of the Dignity Act in 2023, a bipartisan immigration bill, and has reintroduced it.
Wrote the Stop ICE Election Militarization Act to keep immigration enforcement away from elections.

q_federal_spending.summary: Voted against the 2025 reconciliation law, which reduced projected federal Medicaid spending.

q_voting_access.summary: Supports automatic voter registration, early voting and restoring the Voting Rights Act.

q_tariffs.summary: Voted for a resolution to end the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods.

q_legal_status.summary: Authored the Dignity Act, which would create a pathway to legal status for long-term undocumented immigrants.

q_min_wage.summary: Supports raising the minimum wage.

q_abortion.summary: Says she has worked to protect reproductive rights.

candidates.name: Vincent "Vince" Perez
candidates.current_role: State Representative, Texas House District 77, since 2025
candidates.background: Perez represents House District 77 in El Paso and was first elected in 2024. Before joining the House he served two terms as an El Paso County commissioner and chaired the El Paso MPO Transportation Policy Board. He holds undergraduate and graduate degrees in government from Georgetown University and previously worked as a congressional communications director and a public policy adviser.

photo.credit: Official portrait, Texas House of Representatives

priorities.text: Lists fair maps and voting rights as a top priority, including challenging maps he says reduce Hispanic and Black voting power.
Campaigns on creating a public law school in El Paso.
Says he will expand foreign-trained doctor licensure and protect indigent care and county primary care clinics.
Says he will use his Ways and Means seat to push property tax reforms for working-class homeowners, including appraisal cap fairness and expanded homestead protections.
Lists expanding dual credit, strengthening the teacher pipeline, and allowing recall of local school board members.

record.text: Voted against SB 2 (2025), which created a $1 billion education savings account program for private school and homeschool costs; it passed the House 86 to 61.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the school finance and teacher pay bill, on House passage (142 to 5).
Voted for Amendment No. 22 to the 2026-2027 budget (April 2025), which would have directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; it failed 63 to 85.
Voted against SB 17 (2025), restricting land purchases by people and entities tied to designated foreign adversary countries; it passed 86 to 59.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), a proposed constitutional amendment expanding when bail can be denied for certain violent or sexual offenses (adopted 133 to 8).
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail and pretrial release procedures (passed 118 to 25).
Voted against SB 3 (2025), which would have banned most consumable hemp-derived THC products; it passed the House 87 to 54.

Was not recorded voting on SB 8 (2025), requiring agreements between county sheriffs and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to enforce federal immigration law (passed 86 to 47), and stated in the journal that he would have voted no.
Voted against SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms (passed 82 to 46).
Voted against SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders (passed 86 to 53).
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HJR 7 (2025), a constitutional amendment dedicating sales tax revenue to the Texas water fund (122 to 12).
Voted against SB 33 (2025), barring local governments from funding travel for abortions (passed 87 to 58).
Voted against HB 4 (2025, second called session), redrawing Texas congressional districts (passed 88 to 52).
Voted against HB 7 (2025, second called session), prohibiting the manufacture and provision of abortion-inducing drugs and authorizing private lawsuits (passed 82 to 48).
Authored HB 3277 (2025), to adjust the basic allotment and guaranteed yield for inflation; it was referred to committee.
Authored HB 2853 (2025) on a UTEP student union fee, which became law, and joint authored HB 2038 (2025), the DOCTOR Act, on provisional licenses for foreign-trained physicians.

notes.text: Received a 2016 "National County Leader of the Year" recognition from American City & County while a county commissioner, according to his House biography.
Did not respond to the 2024 or 2026 ATPE candidate surveys.
Endorsed by the Texas AFL-CIO COPE for the 2026 general election.

candidates.name: Lizzie Pannill Fletcher
candidates.current_role: U.S. Representative for Texas' 7th District since 2019
candidates.background: Lizzie Pannill Fletcher is a Houston native who graduated from Kenyon College and William and Mary Law School. She practiced law at Vinson and Elkins and became the first woman partner at the Houston firm AZA. She was elected to Congress in 2018 and serves on the Energy and Commerce Committee.

photo.credit: Official portrait, U.S. House of Representatives

priorities.text: Campaigns on restoring reproductive rights in Texas and nationally.
Supports vocational and retraining programs that connect people with high-paying jobs.
Campaigns on flood control and disaster resilience for the Houston area.
Supports comprehensive immigration reform that strengthens border security and penalizes unlawful employers.

record.text: Voted against the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1), the 2025 budget reconciliation law that extended tax cuts and reduced projected federal Medicaid spending, on House passage in May 2025 and final passage in July 2025.
Voted against the Laken Riley Act (S. 5), which requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft-related or certain violent crimes, in January 2025.
Voted against the SAVE Act (H.R. 22), which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections, in April 2025.
Voted against the Protect Children's Innocence Act (H.R. 3492), which would make certain gender transition procedures on minors a federal crime, in December 2025.
Voted against the Do No Harm in Medicaid Act (H.R. 498), which would bar Medicaid funding for gender transition procedures for minors, in December 2025.
Voted for H.J.Res. 72, a resolution to end the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods, in February 2026.
Voted for H.R. 1834, which would extend expanded Affordable Care Act premium tax credits for three years and passed the House 230 to 196, in January 2026.
Voted against the Secure America Act (S. 2), which passed the House on a party-line vote, in June 2026.
Voted against the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (H.R. 7148) in January 2026.
Wrote the Hazard Eligibility and Local Projects Act to let disaster relief projects begin sooner.

candidates.name: Ron Reynolds
candidates.current_role: Texas State Representative, District 27, since 2011
candidates.background: Ron Reynolds of Missouri City has represented House District 27 since 2011. He was previously an associate municipal judge for the City of Houston and president of the Houston Lawyers Association. He chairs the Texas Legislative Black Caucus and founded the Texas House Progressive Caucus.

photo.credit: Official portrait, Texas House of Representatives

priorities.text: Says he is running to fight for stronger public schools, affordable housing and health care.
Lists passing Medicaid expansion, affordable housing, a higher minimum wage and jobs as priorities.
Wants to fully fund public schools and prepare students for an AI-driven workforce.

record.text: Voted against SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on its April 2025 House passage vote.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the House school finance and teacher pay bill.
Voted against the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025), the final version of the school finance bill.
Was absent for the vote on SB 10 (2025), requiring display of the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms; a statement of vote in the journal says the member would have voted no.
Voted against SJR 5 (2025), the constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent felony charges.
Voted against SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations.
Voted against SB 3 (2025), which would have banned consumable hemp-derived THC products (later vetoed by the governor).
Voted against SB 17 (2025), restricting purchases of Texas land by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversary nations.
Was absent for the vote on SB 8 (2025, regular session), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Voted for Amendment No. 22 to the 2025 budget (SB 1), which directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; the amendment failed 63 to 85.
Voted against the 2026-27 state budget (SB 1) on House passage in April 2025.
Voted against SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders.
Was absent for the vote on HB 7 (2025, second called session), allowing civil lawsuits over the manufacture and distribution of abortion-inducing drugs.
In the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker, voted for Dustin Burrows, who was elected Speaker, over David Cook.
In April 2023 voted no on the motion to table, and yes on adoption of, Amendment No. 45 to the budget, which barred state spending on vouchers or similar programs.
Voted for Amendment No. 2 to HB 1 (November 2023), which removed education savings accounts from the bill.
Voted against SB 14 (2023), prohibiting gender transition medical treatments for minors.
Voted against the 2023 motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2127, which limits city and county regulations in fields occupied by state law.
Voted for HR 2377 (May 2023), the articles of impeachment against Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was later acquitted by the Senate.
Voted against SB 3 (fourth called session, 2023), funding border barrier construction and border security operations.
Voted against SB 4 (fourth called session, 2023), creating a state criminal offense for illegal entry from a foreign nation.
Was recorded absent at the August 5, 2025 quorum call, when the House lacked a quorum during the first called session.
Authored HB 726 and HJR 61 (2025) to expand Medicaid eligibility under the Affordable Care Act; neither passed.
Authored HB 812 (2025) on the minimum wage and HB 682 (2025) creating offenses for certain gun show sales; neither passed.
Authored HB 1504 and HJR 70 (2025) to authorize medical cannabis, and HB 4246 (2025) to allow countywide polling places; none passed.

notes.text: In 2015 a jury convicted him of five misdemeanor counts of barratry (illegal solicitation of legal clients), and he was sentenced to one year in jail and a $4,000 fine.
After losing his appeals he served jail time in 2018 and won reelection that November while jailed; misdemeanor convictions do not require a legislator to resign.

candidates.name: Suleman Lalani
candidates.current_role: State Representative, Texas House District 76, since 2023
candidates.background: Lalani is a primary care physician who has practiced in the Sugar Land and greater Houston area for nearly 30 years. He was elected in 2022 to House District 76, which includes Sugar Land, Stafford, Richmond, and Meadows Place. His House biography says he is the first South Asian and first Muslim member of the Texas Legislature and the founder and chair of the Texas Interfaith Legislators Caucus.

photo.credit: Official portrait, Texas House of Representatives

priorities.text: Says improving health care access, especially expanding Medicaid, remains his priority.
Says repealing the private school voucher program is a top education priority.
Says he will keep working to lower prescription drug prices and insurance costs.

promises.text: Says he will refile his bills to weaken insurance companies' control over patient care.

record.text: Voted against SB 2 (2025), which created a $1 billion education savings account program for private school and homeschool costs; it passed the House 86 to 61.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the school finance and teacher pay bill, on House passage (142 to 5).
Voted for Amendment No. 22 to the 2026-2027 budget (April 2025), which would have directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; it failed 63 to 85.
Voted against SB 17 (2025), restricting land purchases by people and entities tied to designated foreign adversary countries; it passed 86 to 59.
Was recorded absent for the vote on SJR 5 (2025), a proposed constitutional amendment expanding when bail can be denied for certain violent or sexual offenses (adopted 133 to 8).
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail and pretrial release procedures (passed 118 to 25).
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned most consumable hemp-derived THC products; it passed the House 87 to 54.
Voted against SB 8 (2025), requiring agreements between county sheriffs and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to enforce federal immigration law (passed 86 to 47).
Voted against SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms (passed 82 to 46).
Voted against SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders (passed 86 to 53).
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HJR 7 (2025), a constitutional amendment dedicating sales tax revenue to the Texas water fund (122 to 12).
Voted against SB 33 (2025), barring local governments from funding travel for abortions (passed 87 to 58).
Voted against HB 4 (2025, second called session), redrawing Texas congressional districts (passed 88 to 52).
Voted against HB 7 (2025, second called session), prohibiting the manufacture and provision of abortion-inducing drugs and authorizing private lawsuits (passed 82 to 48).
Voted against SB 14 (2023), banning gender transition medical treatments for minors (passed 87 to 56).
Voted for the May 2023 resolution impeaching Attorney General Ken Paxton (adopted 121 to 23).
Voted for Amendment No. 45 to the 2023 House budget, barring state money for vouchers or education savings accounts (adopted 86 to 52).
Voted for the November 2023 amendment removing the education savings account program from HB 1 (adopted 84 to 63).
Was recorded absent for the vote on SB 3 (2023, fourth called session), funding border barrier construction and border security operations (passed 84 to 59).
Was recorded absent for the vote on SB 4 (2023, fourth called session), creating a state offense for illegal entry (passed 83 to 61).
Voted against the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2127 (2023), which preempts certain city and county regulation (84 to 58).
Authored HB 397 (2025), requiring a national instant criminal background check for private firearm transfers; it was referred to committee.
Authored HB 891 and HB 1903 (2025), proposing a "Texas solution" alternative program to cover certain low-income people through the private marketplace; both were referred to committee.

notes.text: Endorsed by Texas Parent PAC in the 2022 general election, according to ATPE.
Endorsed by the Texas AFL-CIO COPE for the 2026 general election.

q_vouchers.summary: Calls repealing the voucher program a top priority and voted against SB 2 (2025).

q_school_funding.summary: Voted for HB 2 (2025), the school finance and teacher pay bill.

q_ten_commandments.summary: Voted against SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays in classrooms.

q_medicaid.summary: Says expanding Medicaid eligibility is his priority and voted for the 2025 Medicaid waiver budget amendment.

q_bail.summary: Voted for SB 9 in the 2025 bail legislation (SJR 5 expands bail denial; SB 9 changes pretrial release rules).

q_cannabis.summary: Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned most hemp-derived THC products.

q_foreign_land.summary: Voted against SB 17 (2025), restricting land purchases tied to designated foreign adversaries.

q_deportation.summary: Voted against SB 8 (2025), requiring sheriffs to enter immigration enforcement agreements with ICE.

q_trans_minors.summary: Voted against SB 14 (2023), banning gender transition medical treatments for minors.

q_abortion.summary: Voted against SB 33 and HB 7 of the second called session (2025), which added abortion-related restrictions.

q_gun_laws.summary: Authored HB 397 (2025) to require background checks on private firearm transfers and voted against SB 1362.

q_water.summary: Voted for SB 7 and HJR 7 (2025), creating dedicated water infrastructure funding.

q_preemption.summary: Voted against final approval of HB 2127 (2023), which preempts certain city and county regulation.

issue_notes.summary: Says many families are one medical emergency away from bankruptcy and that he will push to lower prescription prices and premiums.

candidates.name: Surendran K. Pattel
candidates.current_role: Judge, 240th District Court, Fort Bend County, since January 2023
candidates.background: Surendran K. Pattel was born and raised in Kerala, India, and earned his law degree from the University of Calicut in 1995. He practiced as a trial and appellate attorney in India, including before the Supreme Court of India, before moving to the Houston area in 2007. He passed the Texas bar and earned a master's degree in international law from the University of Houston Law Center. He is a certified mediator and practiced in Fort Bend, Harris and Brazoria counties before his election; the county describes him as the first Indian American district judge in Fort Bend County.

priorities.text: Pledges to serve with dignity and respect for all who appear before him.

record.text: Has presided over the 240th District Court since January 1, 2023; the court holds criminal dockets including in-person arraignment and criminal settings.

notes.text: Member of the Exchange Club of Sugar Land and active in Indian American cultural organizations in the Houston area.

candidates.name: Steve Rogers
candidates.current_role: Judge, 268th District Court, Fort Bend County
candidates.background: Steve Rogers is a Houston native and seventh-generation Texan who practiced real estate and tax law for about two decades after an earlier career in sales and insurance. He served as senior counsel and general counsel to multinational companies, practiced in Arizona and federal courts, and later worked as a lawyer in the oil-services industry. He holds a business degree from Baylor University, an MBA from Pepperdine University, a law degree from Trinity Law School and an LLM from Regent University School of Law. He lives in Fort Bend County with his wife and four children and raises sheep on a farm in Needville.

priorities.text: Says he is running to keep criminals off the streets, enforce the law and get the justice system back to work.
Says he will follow the law as written and will not rewrite the law from the bench.
Campaigns on fair and speedy trials and clearing case backlogs.
Says he ran and won on a 'Tired of Crime' platform and works to move as many criminal cases as he can.

record.text: Says he has disposed of more than 35 sexual assault cases since taking the bench, many involving young victims.
In December 2025 he sentenced Timothy Carroll to 25 years in prison after guilty pleas to aggravated sexual assault of a child, as reported by the Fort Bend Star and cited by his campaign.
Appointed Maggie Jaramillo as his associate judge (2023 to 2024) and later appointed former child abuse prosecutor Craig Priesmeyer as associate judge in 2025.

notes.text: The county court page says he was diagnosed with cancer after taking the bench and believes he is now cancer free.

q_textualism.summary: Says a judge's duty is to follow the law as it is written and apply it fairly, not to make, rewrite or bend the law to fit public opinion.

candidates.name: Daniel Wong
candidates.current_role: Interim Fort Bend County Judge since April 2026 (appointment disputed); president and CEO, Tolunay-Wong Engineers
candidates.background: Daniel Wong, originally from Macau, is a civil engineer who earned bachelor's, master's and doctoral degrees from the University of Houston and leads Tolunay-Wong Engineers, a firm he says employs more than 400 people. He served on the Sugar Land City Council from 2002 to 2008 and on the Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board. He won the March 2026 Republican primary with about 54 percent, defeating incumbent KP George, and was named interim county judge in April 2026 after a visiting judge suspended George in a civil case. He is an elder at Fort Bend Community Church and lives in Sugar Land.

priorities.text: Says he is running to lower property taxes so tax bills go down, not just grow more slowly.
Campaigns on attracting employers to grow the commercial tax base and streamlining small business permitting.
Campaigns on infrastructure and flood protection, including repaving neglected roads and holding developers accountable for infrastructure.
Campaigns on workforce development, including skilled trades and apprenticeships.
Says he will support law enforcement and first responders and reduce crime through prevention and enforcement.
Says his priority is managing growth while protecting taxpayers and essential services.

promises.text: Says he will use the office to advocate for a cap on appraisal increases and to stop 'backdoor tax increases.'
Says he will audit government waste and prioritize fiscal discipline.
Says he will work with local authorities for reliable access to safe drinking water for all residents.

record.text: Was named interim county judge on April 10, 2026, after visiting Judge Jeth Jones suspended KP George in a civil case over residents' First Amendment complaints; the appointment was to last through that case.

After the civil case was dismissed in June 2026, the county attorney said his appointment ended June 17; he continued presiding, citing the Texas Constitution's holdover provision, and two commissioners voted to keep him presiding.

Filed suit against County Attorney Bridgette Smith-Lawson, arguing she exceeded her authority by declaring his appointment over; his attorneys say Commissioners Court approved his appointment through the end of 2026.
Says the county lowered its tax rate from 41.2 to 40.7 cents during his tenure.
Hired Trever Nehls as chief of staff at a six-figure salary, which Dexter McCoy said was more than double what other court employees earn.

notes.text: Endorsed by Gov. Greg Abbott, according to his campaign.
The Houston Chronicle editorial board endorsed him in the Republican primary; it endorsed his opponent in the general election.
A Texas Southern University poll conducted September 9 to October 2, 2026 found McCoy at 49 percent and Wong at 40 percent among registered voters.

q_county_tax.summary: Pledges to lower property tax bills, not just slow their growth, and says he would manage growth without raising taxes by seeking outside funding and growing the commercial base.

candidates.current_role: Fort Bend County Commissioner, Precinct 4, since January 2023
candidates.background: Dexter McCoy grew up in Mission Bend and earned a degree in broadcast journalism and political science from Boston University. He won the May 26, 2026 Democratic runoff for county judge with about 74 percent over Rachelle Carter. He is married with two daughters.

priorities.text: Says his top priority is affordability, including targeted tax relief and growing the commercial tax base so infrastructure costs are not placed solely on homeowners and renters.
Campaigns on 'bringing back ethical leadership,' including an open budget process and zero tolerance for corruption.
Campaigns on better transportation, congestion relief and expanded transit options.
Says he will require county contractors to pay a living wage and promote worker safety standards.
Campaigns on supporting early childhood education and union apprenticeship programs.

promises.text: Says he will expand his budget town halls from Precinct 4 to the entire county.
Says he will initiate a countywide development plan to serve as a roadmap for future growth.
Says he will encourage the county to join or support lawsuits when state or federal actions violate voting rights or local authority.

record.text: As commissioner, says he helped raise the minimum wage for county employees, passed the county's first paid parental leave policy and nearly doubled paid sick time.
Says he launched a mobility dashboard and a countywide 311 system and has held nearly 40 town halls in Precinct 4.
In June 2026 he and Commissioner Grady Prestage walked out of a Commissioners Court meeting, saying the court lacked a legal quorum because they do not recognize Daniel Wong as acting county judge.
Opposed the appointment of Daniel Wong as interim county judge and criticized Wong's hiring of a chief of staff at a six-figure salary as 'completely wasting taxpayer dollars.'

notes.text: Endorsed by U.S. Reps. Lizzie Fletcher and Christian Menefee and state Reps. Gene Wu, Jon Rosenthal and James Talarico; the Houston Chronicle endorsed him in the primary and the general election.

candidates.current_role: Texas State Representative, District 24, since 2013; chair of the House Appropriations Committee
candidates.background: Greg Bonnen of Friendswood is a practicing neurosurgeon and chairman of the board of Houston Physicians' Hospital. He has represented House District 24 since 2013 and chairs the House Appropriations Committee. He grew up in Angleton and graduated from Texas A&M University.

photo.credit: Official portrait, Texas House of Representatives

priorities.text: Names affordability, including property taxes and home, auto and health insurance costs, as the biggest challenge.
Wants education funding to reach classrooms and public universities to stay affordable, with more STEM and vocational programs.
Supports investment in water, transportation, drainage and flood control infrastructure.
Cites denying bail to criminal illegal immigrants charged with felonies as a public safety priority.

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on its April 2025 House passage vote.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the House school finance and teacher pay bill.
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025), the final version of the school finance bill.
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring display of the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), the constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent felony charges.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned consumable hemp-derived THC products (later vetoed by the governor).
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting purchases of Texas land by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversary nations.
Voted for SB 8 (2025, regular session), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Voted against Amendment No. 22 to the 2025 budget (SB 1), which directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; the amendment failed 63 to 85.
Voted for the 2026-27 state budget (SB 1) on House passage in April 2025.
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders.
Voted for HB 7 (2025, second called session), allowing civil lawsuits over the manufacture and distribution of abortion-inducing drugs.
In the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker, voted for Dustin Burrows, who was elected Speaker, over David Cook.
In April 2023 voted yes on the motion to table, and no on adoption of, Amendment No. 45 to the budget, which barred state spending on vouchers or similar programs.
Voted against Amendment No. 2 to HB 1 (November 2023), which removed education savings accounts from the bill.
Voted for SB 14 (2023), prohibiting gender transition medical treatments for minors.
Voted for the 2023 motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2127, which limits city and county regulations in fields occupied by state law.
Voted for HR 2377 (May 2023), the articles of impeachment against Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was later acquitted by the Senate.
Voted for SB 3 (fourth called session, 2023), funding border barrier construction and border security operations.
Voted for SB 4 (fourth called session, 2023), creating a state criminal offense for illegal entry from a foreign nation.
Authored HB 500 (2025), the supplemental appropriations bill, which became law.
Authored HB 130 (2025), on genetic information security, HB 3812 (2025), on health plan preauthorization, and HB 4638 (2025), on the Texas Pharmaceutical Initiative; all became law.

notes.text: His House biography lists recognition as a Texas Values Faith and Family Champion and as a Pro-Life Hero.

candidates.name: Mark Henry
candidates.current_role: Galveston County Judge since 2011
candidates.background: Mark Henry was elected Galveston County Judge in 2010, the first Republican to hold the office since Reconstruction, and took office in 2011; he is seeking a fifth term. He defeated Chris Kinard in the March 2026 Republican primary with about 67 percent. He was an original chairman of the Gulf Coast Community Protection and Recovery District, formed after Hurricane Ike to study a coastal barrier.

priorities.text: Campaigns on lower taxes, public safety, less government and more efficiency, emergency management and infrastructure.
Says permanent drainage solutions will require federal, state and regional partnerships and billions of dollars of investment.

record.text: Says the county has adopted a property tax rate below the no-new-revenue rate every year since 2011, cutting the rate from about 0.63 to 0.32 per $100 valuation by 2025.
Says the county paid down debt and earned its first Aaa bond rating.
Says the Commissioners Court completed a countywide drainage study in 2021 and has spent hundreds of millions of dollars on road and drainage projects.
In 2021 the county declared a disaster over fentanyl deaths, created a Southern Border Taskforce that sent deputies to the border, and joined Operation Lone Star until it stood down in April 2025.
Says he increased the number of sheriff's and constable's officers on the streets.

notes.text: Galveston County, with Henry as a named defendant, was sued over the 2021 commissioners precinct map; a federal district court found it violated Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, and on August 1, 2024 the full Fifth Circuit reversed that ruling.
Won the March 3, 2026 Republican primary with about 67 percent of the vote over Chris Kinard.

q_county_tax.summary: Says the county has set its tax rate below the no-new-revenue rate every year since 2011, cutting the rate by nearly half, while urging voters to elect fiscally conservative local officials.

candidates.background: Luther represents a Grayson County district. She defeated then-Rep. Reggie Smith in the 2024 Republican primary after losing to him in 2022, and ran unsuccessfully in a 2020 special election for Senate District 30. She ran unopposed in the 2026 Republican primary.

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program; it passed the House 86 to 61.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the main public school finance bill, on third reading; it passed 142 to 5.
Voted against the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025 school finance); it prevailed 122 to 13.
Voted against a 2025 budget amendment by Rep. John Bucy directing the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; it failed 63 to 85.
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting land purchases by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversary countries; it passed 86 to 59.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), a constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent offenses; it was adopted 133 to 8.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations; it passed 118 to 25.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned most consumable hemp-derived THC products, on second reading; it advanced 95 to 44.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), the hemp-derived THC products bill, on third reading; it passed 87 to 54.
Voted for SB 33 (2025), barring local governments from funding travel for abortion services; it passed 87 to 58.
Voted for SB 8 (2025), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement; it passed 86 to 47.
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms; it passed 82 to 46.
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting the recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders; it passed 86 to 53.
Voted against the conference report on SB 1, the 2026-2027 state budget; it was adopted 107 to 21.
Voted for HB 4 (2025 second called session), redrawing Texas congressional districts; it passed 88 to 52.
Voted for HB 7 (2025 second called session), restricting abortion-inducing drugs; it passed 82 to 48.
Authored HB 3441 (2025) on the liability of vaccine manufacturers that advertise a harmful vaccine, which became law.
Joint author of HB 2657 (2025), proposing to abolish the Texas Education Agency.

notes.text: Endorsed in the 2024 Republican primary by Gov. Greg Abbott, according to ATPE.

record.text: Voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1), the 2025 budget reconciliation law that extended tax cuts and reduced projected federal Medicaid spending, on House passage in May 2025 and final passage in July 2025.

candidates.name: Jay Dean
candidates.current_role: Texas State Representative, District 7, since 2017
candidates.background: Jay Dean of Longview has represented House District 7 since 2017. He served a decade as mayor of Longview and five years on the city council. He is general manager of Thomas Oilfield Services and a graduate of Louisiana State University.

photo.credit: Official portrait, Texas House of Representatives

priorities.text: Describes himself as an advocate for smaller government, responsible budgeting, low tax rates and a business-friendly environment.
Lists strengthening public education and workforce training, the right to life and the Second Amendment among his priorities.

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on its April 2025 House passage vote.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the House school finance and teacher pay bill.
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025), the final version of the school finance bill.
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring display of the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), the constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent felony charges.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned consumable hemp-derived THC products (later vetoed by the governor).
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting purchases of Texas land by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversary nations.
Voted for SB 8 (2025, regular session), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Voted against Amendment No. 22 to the 2025 budget (SB 1), which directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; the amendment failed 63 to 85.
Voted for the 2026-27 state budget (SB 1) on House passage in April 2025.
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders.
Voted for HB 7 (2025, second called session), allowing civil lawsuits over the manufacture and distribution of abortion-inducing drugs.
In the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker, voted for Dustin Burrows, who was elected Speaker, over David Cook.
In April 2023 voted no on the motion to table, and yes on adoption of, Amendment No. 45 to the budget, which barred state spending on vouchers or similar programs.
Voted for Amendment No. 2 to HB 1 (November 2023), which removed education savings accounts from the bill.
Voted for SB 14 (2023), prohibiting gender transition medical treatments for minors.
Voted for the 2023 motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2127, which limits city and county regulations in fields occupied by state law.
Voted for HR 2377 (May 2023), the articles of impeachment against Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was later acquitted by the Senate.
Voted for SB 3 (fourth called session, 2023), funding border barrier construction and border security operations.
Voted for SB 4 (fourth called session, 2023), creating a state criminal offense for illegal entry from a foreign nation.
Authored HB 138 (2025), creating the Health Impact, Cost, and Coverage Analysis Program, which became law.
Authored HB 3619 (2025), on surface owner rights when the Railroad Commission plugs wells, and HB 2686 (2025), requiring registration of frac tanks; both became law.

notes.text: In the 2024 ATPE survey he said he would support vouchers "only if someone can show me how we find it in perpetuity" and without cuts to public schools; he voted for SB 2 in 2025.
In the 2024 ATPE survey he said "if we want the best schools we need to fully fund them" and supported a state-funded raise for educators.

candidates.background: Bert Richardson has served on the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals since 2015 and is leaving that statewide seat to run for chief justice of the San Antonio-based Fourth Court of Appeals. record.text: Voted against the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1), the 2025 budget reconciliation law that extended tax cuts and reduced projected federal Medicaid spending, on House passage in May 2025 and final passage in July 2025.
Voted against the Laken Riley Act (S. 5), which requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft-related or certain violent crimes, in January 2025.
Voted against the SAVE Act (H.R. 22), which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections, in April 2025.
Voted against the Protect Children's Innocence Act (H.R. 3492), which would make certain gender transition procedures on minors a federal crime, in December 2025.
Voted against the Do No Harm in Medicaid Act (H.R. 498), which would bar Medicaid funding for gender transition procedures for minors, in December 2025.
Voted for H.J.Res. 72, a resolution to end the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods, in February 2026.
Voted for H.R. 1834, which would extend expanded Affordable Care Act premium tax credits for three years and passed the House 230 to 196, in January 2026.
Voted against the Secure America Act (S. 2), which passed the House on a party-line vote, in June 2026.

record.text: Authored HB 1657 (2025) to create an education savings account program and HJR 84 (2025) to let the Legislature set minimum bonds for certain violent felonies; neither passed.

has not committed to extending the county's Flock camera contract and says camera data should be limited to law enforcement use with no third-party sharing or sale.

has called for investigations and transparency in ICE operations, according to the Chronicle.

candidates.name: Letitia Plummer
candidates.current_role: Dentist; former Houston City Council member, At-Large Position 4 (2020 to 2025)
candidates.background: Letitia Plummer is a dentist and small business owner who served on the Houston City Council in At-Large Position 4 from 2020 through 2025. She ran unsuccessfully for Congress in 2018. She won the 2026 Democratic nomination for county judge by defeating former Houston Mayor Annise Parker in a May runoff.

priorities.text: Says it is time for the county to "tighten the belt" and examine where it spends the most money, while seeking more state and federal infrastructure funding.

Names justice (including expanding Cite and Release and non-police emergency response), a county housing trust fund, and funding Harris Health clinics and behavioral health services as top priorities.
Calls disaster resilience her primary priority, including neighborhood resilience hubs that can operate off the grid.
Wants to continue county services beyond infrastructure and public safety, including mental health, financial literacy, and small business support.

promises.text: Says she would not renew or would cancel the county's Flock license plate camera contract as written and would require published use policies, audits, and data limits.
Pledged at an October 2026 forum to support raising $1 million for at least three new community lighthouse resilience hubs and full funding for Harris Health.
Pledged to seek future flood control bond elections once 2018 bond funds are spent.
Says she would create a dedicated County Housing Trust Fund and offer down payment assistance for first-time homebuyers.

record.text: On the Houston City Council, pushed a police reform proposal, tenant protections for substandard apartments, and limits on Houston Police Department cooperation with federal immigration agents.
Says she secured funding for the first generator at the Kashmere Gardens Multipurpose Center while on the council.

notes.text: Finished second in the March 2026 Democratic primary with 37.3 percent and won the May runoff with 51.1 percent over Annise Parker.

The Chronicle editorial board endorsed her (3.5 of 5 stars), and noted she has filed faulty campaign finance reports and was sanctioned twice by the Texas State Board of Dental Examiners, most recently in 2022.
A University of Houston Hobby School survey released October 13, 2026 showed Plummer at 47 percent to 40 percent for Sanchez among likely voters.
In the Houston Bar Association's 2026 poll (not an endorsement), Plummer received 271 votes to 282 for Orlando Sanchez.

q_county_tax.summary: Opposed the 2026 county property tax increase and supports finding efficiencies, but declined to commit to lowering the rate and said she would not cut county programs.

q_county_mental.summary: Lists expanding behavioral health services and non-police emergency response among her top priorities and wants the county to keep funding mental health services.

issue_notes.summary: supports building a new, fully staffed and more humane jail rather than a larger one, while reducing the jail population and speeding case processing.
proposes bringing in more small and midsize contractors, paying them promptly, and planning better around state and federal funding rules.
wrote that the county should comply with the letter of the law on immigration enforcement and not go beyond its requirements.
criticized using temporary COVID-era federal funds for permanent programs and says residents should have been told when programs relied on temporary funding.

candidates.background: Sonia Lopez was appointed judge of Harris County Civil Court at Law No. 1 by Commissioners Court in December 2025, after Judge Audrie Lawton-Evans stepped down to run for county attorney. Earlier in her career she interned for then-Commissioner Sylvia Garcia and served as chief of staff for state Rep. Ana Hernandez.

priorities.text: Says her court has averaged a clearance rate over 100 percent and adds extra dockets as needed to address its caseload.

record.text: Appointed judge of County Civil Court at Law No. 1 by Harris County Commissioners Court on December 11, 2025.

notes.text: In the Houston Bar Association 2026 Judicial Preference Poll (769 ballots; not an HBA endorsement), Sonia Lopez received 152 votes and Jamie King received 124.

candidates.name: Leslie R. Johnson
candidates.current_role: Judge, Harris County Criminal Court at Law No. 3 since 2023
candidates.background: Leslie R. Johnson has been judge of Harris County Criminal Court at Law No. 3 since January 2023. She is a Republican and is seeking reelection.

priorities.text: Says she runs one of the most efficient courts in the county with some of the lowest misdemeanor docket numbers.
Says everyone in her court is treated the same and provided equal opportunity regardless of financial means.

record.text: Is one of four Republican misdemeanor judges who, with Attorney General Ken Paxton, sought to undo the 2019 ODonnell bail consent decree; a federal judge rejected the request in 2026.

The court-appointed monitor's Ninth Report (March 3, 2026) in the federal ODonnell misdemeanor bail case described three cases in her Court Three, one from October 2025 and two from January 2026, in which general order bonds were revoked or replaced with secured bonds at first appearance for defendants not yet represented by counsel, and stated that these actions violated Local Rule 9 and the Consent Decree. The Houston Chronicle editorial board reported that she called the report "slanderous."

notes.text: In the Houston Bar Association 2026 Judicial Preference Poll (769 ballots; not an HBA endorsement), Leslie R. Johnson received 129 votes and Carlos Alberto Aguayo received 105.

issue_notes.summary: Says defendants should not be jailed simply because they cannot afford bail, but objects that most Class A and B misdemeanor defendants receive general order bonds without regard to criminal history, which she says violates state law.

candidates.name: Abbie Kamin
candidates.current_role: Harris County Attorney since June 2026 (appointed)
candidates.background: Abbie Kamin is a Houston native and civil rights attorney who focused on voting rights and later served as an associate regional director for the Anti-Defamation League. She represented District C on Houston City Council from 2020 until her candidacy for this office required her to leave the council under Texas's resign-to-run law. Commissioners Court appointed her county attorney in April 2026 on a 3-2 vote, effective June 15, after Christian Menefee left for Congress; she is the first woman to hold the office.

priorities.text: Lists protecting vulnerable children and seniors, safe and healthy neighborhoods, disaster and flood response, voting rights and clean air and water as priorities.
Says she will take on deed fraud scammers, polluters, slumlords and domestic abusers.
Says the office must vigorously defend the county against what she calls hostile attacks by Gov. Greg Abbott and President Donald Trump.

record.text: Her office joined El Paso, Dallas and Travis counties in a successful lawsuit against the federal government that preserved $23.3 million in national security funds for the Houston region, according to the Chronicle.
Successfully challenged the EPA's termination of a clean-energy grant, recovering $54 million for Harris County solar initiatives, according to the Chronicle.
Launched an in-house Family Division and, with the district attorney, expanded free protective-order services for domestic violence survivors.

On City Council, created the Houston Women's Commission, secured paid parental leave for city employees, launched a firearm injury dashboard and created the Office of Policing Reform and Accountability.

notes.text: The Houston Chronicle editorial board endorsed Abbie Kamin in this race.
In the Houston Bar Association 2026 Judicial Preference Poll (769 ballots; not an HBA endorsement), Abbie Kamin received 350 votes and Jacqueline Lucci Smith received 191.
Narrowly defeated Civil Court at Law Judge Audrie Lawton-Evans in the March 2026 Democratic primary.
Commissioners Rodney Ellis, Lesley Briones and Adrian Garcia voted for her appointment; Tom Ramsey and Lina Hidalgo voted against, with Hidalgo citing concerns about interim appointments.

issue_notes.summary: Says local control is being targeted by state and federal leaders and that her office will stand firm; says she is the only candidate who has defeated Greg Abbott in court.

Wants to work with the Legislature and the Texas Department of Insurance to lower property insurance rates.

promises.text: Says the county must rebuild its depleted disaster reserve fund and restrict it to disaster-related events.

record.text: Says that during his last 20 years on Commissioners Court the county tax rate was not raised, there was no budget deficit and the county held a AAA bond rating.
Cites a Precinct 3 park system of more than 60 parks on 15,000 acres and 68 miles of trails built during his tenure.

notes.text: A University of Houston Hobby School poll of likely voters conducted October 3 to 8, 2026, found Briones at 49 percent and Radack at 41 percent.

The Houston Chronicle, which endorsed his opponent, recalled a past remark of his that some residents "enjoy floods," which he later walked back, and cost growth at the Hockley Derby Park he championed.
Was unopposed in the March 2026 Republican primary.

q_county_tax.summary: Says reducing property taxes is a priority, criticizes a 17.6 percent rise in county property taxes over two years, and opposes new programs taxpayers must fund.

issue_notes.summary: Says 2018 flood bond projects have been delayed and revised, that some downstream projects were discarded, and that the court must work with the new flood control director to finish them.
Says the county wasted millions over six years on new administrative departments and faces a projected budget deficit.

candidates.name: Lesley Briones
candidates.current_role: Harris County Commissioner, Precinct 4, since 2023

priorities.text: Says nothing is more important than public safety and cites pay parity for county law enforcement and more resources for the district attorney.

record.text: Voted on September 17, 2026, for a county tax rate increase of about 7.6 percent, estimated at $193 more a year for the average homeowner, saying it was "in the best interests of the people of Harris County."

Says the county required backup power at nursing homes and assisted living facilities.
Moved to nominate Abbie Kamin as interim county attorney in April 2026, which Commissioners Court approved.
Led Commissioners Court in approving compensation increases for top staff in her office, according to the Chronicle; she says those staff deliver more services.

notes.text: The Houston Chronicle editorial board endorsed Lesley Briones in this race.

q_county_mental.summary: Says she championed more resources for mental health services and was a major backer of the HART 911 mental health diversion program.

issue_notes.summary: Says Harris County is squeezed by state decisions such as not expanding Medicaid and a new tax exemption that removed $8 billion from county rolls, according to the Chronicle.

candidates.name: Erin Zwiener
candidates.current_role: State Representative, Texas House District 45, since 2019
candidates.background: Zwiener describes herself as an attorney, conservationist and educator and is founder and chair of the Texas Energy and Climate Caucus. She was first elected in 2018 and is seeking a fourth full term representing part of Hays County. She has served on the Natural Resources Committee and as vice chair of an Appropriations subcommittee on education.

photo.credit: Official portrait, Texas House of Representatives

priorities.text: Seeks more local authority for counties to manage growth and protect natural resources.
Lists improving water conservation standards and funding local groundwater districts as priorities.
Lists increasing state funding for public schools as a priority.
Lists expanding Medicaid and decreasing maternal mortality as priorities.
Lists addressing climate change through mitigation and adaptation and strengthening separation of church and state.

promises.text: Says she will work to end tax incentives for data centers, regulate their water, energy use and noise, and let counties reject industrial developments.

record.text: Voted against SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program; it passed the House 86 to 61.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the main public school finance bill, on third reading; it passed 142 to 5.
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025 school finance); it prevailed 122 to 13.
Voted for a 2025 budget amendment by Rep. John Bucy directing the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; it failed 63 to 85.
Voted against SB 17 (2025), restricting land purchases by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversary countries; it passed 86 to 59.
Voted against SJR 5 (2025), a constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent offenses; it was adopted 133 to 8.
Voted against SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations; it passed 118 to 25.
Voted against SB 3 (2025), which would have banned most consumable hemp-derived THC products, on second reading; it advanced 95 to 44.
Voted against SB 3 (2025), the hemp-derived THC products bill, on third reading; it passed 87 to 54.
Voted against SB 33 (2025), barring local governments from funding travel for abortion services; it passed 87 to 58.
Voted against SB 8 (2025), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement; it passed 86 to 47.
Voted against SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms; it passed 82 to 46.
Voted against SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting the recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders; it passed 86 to 53.
Voted for the conference report on SB 1, the 2026-2027 state budget; it was adopted 107 to 21.
Voted against HB 4 (2025 second called session), redrawing Texas congressional districts; it passed 88 to 52.
Voted against HB 7 (2025 second called session), restricting abortion-inducing drugs; it passed 82 to 48.
Voted for a 2023 budget amendment (Amendment No. 45 to HB 1) barring the use of state funds for school vouchers or similar programs; it was adopted 86 to 52.
Voted for the November 2023 amendment offered by Rep. John Raney, Rep. Drew Darby and others that struck the education savings account program from HB 1; it was adopted 84 to 63.
Voted against SB 14 (2023), banning gender transition medical treatments for minors; it passed 87 to 56.
Voted for HR 2377 (2023), impeaching Attorney General Ken Paxton; it was adopted 121 to 23.
Voted against SB 3 (2023 fourth called session), funding state border barrier construction; it passed 84 to 59.
Voted against SB 4 (2023 fourth called session), creating a state offense for illegal entry from a foreign nation; it passed 83 to 61.
Authored HB 1020 (2025), setting campaign contribution limits for certain offices; it did not advance past committee.
Authored HB 2019 (2025), expanding Medicaid eligibility to certain adults younger than 26; it did not advance past committee.
Authored HB 2347 (2025) on county water conservation programs, which passed the House.

notes.text: Endorsed by the Texas AFL-CIO COPE for the 2026 general election.
Endorsed in 2022 by Texas Parent PAC and by the Austin American-Statesman editorial board, according to ATPE.

q_vouchers.summary: Voted against SB 2 (2025) and for 2023 amendments blocking voucher funding; told ATPE in 2022 that public dollars should stay in public schools.

q_school_funding.summary: Lists increasing state funding to public schools as a priority and voted for HB 2 (2025).

q_ten_commandments.summary: Voted against SB 10 (2025) and lists strengthening separation of church and state as a priority.

q_medicaid.summary: Voted for the 2025 Medicaid expansion waiver amendment, authored a bill expanding Medicaid to certain young adults and lists expanding Medicaid as a priority.

q_bail.summary: Voted against SJR 5 and against SB 9, the 2025 bail measures.

q_cannabis.summary: Voted against SB 3 (2025), which would have banned most hemp-derived THC products.

q_foreign_land.summary: Voted against SB 17 (2025), restricting land purchases tied to designated foreign adversaries.

q_abortion.summary: Voted against SB 33 (2025) and against HB 7 (2025), both measures restricting abortion access.

q_gun_laws.summary: Voted against SB 1362 (2025), which bars enforcement of extreme risk protective orders.

q_deportation.summary: Voted against SB 8 (2025), requiring sheriff agreements with ICE; voted against SB 4 (2023), creating a state illegal entry offense. No direct statement on deportation priorities was found.

q_border_state.summary: Voted against SB 3 (2023) border barrier funding and says she will work to end what she calls border shenanigans that slowed trade.

q_trans_minors.summary: Voted against SB 14 (2023), the ban on gender transition treatments for minors.

q_ethics.summary: Authored HB 1020 (2025) to set campaign contribution limits for certain offices.

q_preemption.summary: Seeks more authority for Hays County to manage growth and for counties to reject industrial developments.

q_water.summary: Says the state has invested in new water projects and must also repair old infrastructure and raise conservation standards.

issue_notes.summary: Says she will work to ensure industrial developments joining the Texas grid pay their own way and do not raise utility costs.

candidates.name: Monica De La Cruz
candidates.current_role: U.S. Representative for Texas' 15th District since 2023
candidates.background: Monica De La Cruz is a former insurance agent who owned an insurance agency in the Rio Grande Valley. She was elected in 2022 as the first Latina and first Republican to represent the 15th District. She created the South Texas Water Working Group.

photo.credit: Official portrait, U.S. House of Representatives (Office of the Clerk)

priorities.text: Calls for completing border infrastructure and reinstating the Remain in Mexico policy.
Supports oil and natural gas jobs, cutting regulations that raise energy costs and the safe use of nuclear energy.
Pledges to protect Medicare and Social Security.
Presses Mexico to meet its water treaty obligations to South Texas farmers.

record.text: Voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1), the 2025 budget reconciliation law that extended tax cuts and reduced projected federal Medicaid spending, on House passage in May 2025 and final passage in July 2025.
Voted for the Laken Riley Act (S. 5), which requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft-related or certain violent crimes, in January 2025.
Did not vote on the SAVE Act (H.R. 22), which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections, in April 2025.
Voted for the Protect Children's Innocence Act (H.R. 3492), which would make certain gender transition procedures on minors a federal crime, in December 2025.
Voted for the Do No Harm in Medicaid Act (H.R. 498), which would bar Medicaid funding for gender transition procedures for minors, in December 2025.
Voted against H.J.Res. 72, a resolution to end the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods, in February 2026.
Voted for H.R. 1834, which would extend expanded Affordable Care Act premium tax credits for three years and passed the House 230 to 196, in January 2026.
Voted for the Secure America Act (S. 2), which passed the House on a party-line vote, in June 2026.
Voted for the Born-Alive Abortion Survivors Protection Act (H.R. 21) in January 2025.
Voted for the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (H.R. 7148) in January 2026.
Was the only Texas Republican to vote for a three-year extension of expanded ACA premium tax credits in January 2026.
Sponsored the SPEAK Act on telehealth access for people with limited English, which became law as part of a broader spending package.
Introduced the Water Assurance and Treaty Enforcement for Rio Grande Farmers Act, which would place tariffs on Mexico if it fails to meet water treaty deliveries.
Secured passage of legislation targeting fentanyl trafficking, according to her campaign.

notes.text: Endorsed by President Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson.

q_federal_spending.summary: Voted for the 2025 reconciliation law and backs a balanced budget amendment, but also voted to extend ACA subsidies.

q_trans_minors.summary: Voted for a bill to make certain gender transition procedures on minors a federal crime and for a ban on Medicaid funding for such procedures for minors.

q_tariffs.summary: Opposes tariffs that hinder farmers' exports but has proposed tariffs on Mexico over water treaty violations, and voted against ending the Canada tariff emergency.

q_fossil_priority.summary: Supports oil and natural gas jobs and nuclear energy and opposes regulations that raise energy costs.

issue_notes.summary: Says she has worked across the aisle to lower health care costs and require prescription drug price transparency.

photo.credit: Official portrait, U.S. House of Representatives

priorities.text: Proposes direct refund payments to offset tariff-driven price increases.
Supports securing the border and deporting violent criminals without detaining children and longtime residents with families.
Calls for eliminating provisions that reduce people's Social Security benefits.
Supports border technology, modernized ports of entry and more personnel.

record.text: Voted against the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1), the 2025 budget reconciliation law that extended tax cuts and reduced projected federal Medicaid spending, on House passage in May 2025 and final passage in July 2025.
Voted for the Laken Riley Act (S. 5), which requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft-related or certain violent crimes, in January 2025.
Voted for the SAVE Act (H.R. 22), which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections, in April 2025.
Voted for the Protect Children's Innocence Act (H.R. 3492), which would make certain gender transition procedures on minors a federal crime, in December 2025.
Voted for the Do No Harm in Medicaid Act (H.R. 498), which would bar Medicaid funding for gender transition procedures for minors, in December 2025.
Voted for H.J.Res. 72, a resolution to end the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods, in February 2026.
Voted for H.R. 1834, which would extend expanded Affordable Care Act premium tax credits for three years and passed the House 230 to 196, in January 2026.
Voted against the Secure America Act (S. 2), which passed the House on a party-line vote, in June 2026.
Voted for the Born-Alive Abortion Survivors Protection Act (H.R. 21) in January 2025.
Voted for the Department of Homeland Security Appropriations Act, 2026 (H.R. 7744) in March 2026.
Helped pass the 2021 bipartisan infrastructure law, which funded transportation projects in the district, according to his campaign.
Cosponsored the Farm Workforce Modernization Act of 2019 on agricultural worker visas and status.

notes.text: Was indicted in 2024 on federal bribery and money laundering charges, which he denied; President Trump pardoned him in December 2025.
Endorsed by Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries; LUPE Votes endorsed him with conditions.

candidates.background: Ashby is a community banker from Lufkin with a degree in agricultural economics from Texas A&M University. record.text: Voted for and cosponsored SB 2 (2025), creating education savings accounts.
