record.text: Voted against SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on its April 2025 House passage vote.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the House school finance and teacher pay bill.

Was absent for the vote on the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025), the final version of the school finance bill; a statement of vote in the journal says the member would have voted yes.
Voted against SB 10 (2025), requiring display of the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), the constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent felony charges.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned consumable hemp-derived THC products (later vetoed by the governor).
Was absent for the vote on SB 17 (2025), restricting purchases of Texas land by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversary nations.
Voted against SB 8 (2025, regular session), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Voted for Amendment No. 22 to the 2025 budget (SB 1), which directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; the amendment failed 63 to 85.
Voted for the 2026-27 state budget (SB 1) on House passage in April 2025.
Voted against SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders.
Voted against HB 7 (2025, second called session), allowing civil lawsuits over the manufacture and distribution of abortion-inducing drugs.
In the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker, voted for Dustin Burrows, who was elected Speaker, over David Cook.
In April 2023 voted no on the motion to table, and yes on adoption of, Amendment No. 45 to the budget, which barred state spending on vouchers or similar programs.
Voted for Amendment No. 2 to HB 1 (November 2023), which removed education savings accounts from the bill.
Voted against SB 14 (2023), prohibiting gender transition medical treatments for minors.
Voted against the 2023 motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2127, which limits city and county regulations in fields occupied by state law.
Voted for HR 2377 (May 2023), the articles of impeachment against Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was later acquitted by the Senate.
Voted against SB 3 (fourth called session, 2023), funding border barrier construction and border security operations.
Voted against SB 4 (fourth called session, 2023), creating a state criminal offense for illegal entry from a foreign nation.
Was recorded absent at the August 5, 2025 quorum call, when the House lacked a quorum during the first called session.

Authored HB 1188 (2025), on information about intellectual and developmental disability services for parents of special education students, and HB 3745 (2025), on crime victims' compensation; both became law.
Authored HB 1201 (2025), a pilot program for Medicaid coverage of doula services; it did not pass.
Voted against tabling the April 2025 amendment that would have put the voucher program to a statewide vote, according to ATPE.

candidates.current_role: Chief Justice, Ninth Court of Appeals, since January 1, 2021
candidates.background: Scott Golemon became chief justice of the Beaumont-based Ninth Court of Appeals on January 1, 2021. He spent more than 30 years as a civil trial and appellate lawyer in Montgomery County and the surrounding region, at firms including Haas & Golemon (1997 to 2011) and Hope & Causey (2012 to 2020), and says he handled about 300 jury trials. He earned B.S. and M.S. degrees in agricultural education from Tarleton State University (1983 and 1984) and a J.D. from the University of Houston (1987). He is a past president of the Montgomery County Bar Association.

priorities.text: Said in a 2020 candidate statement that he would follow and enforce the laws and would not legislate from the bench.
Said a justice's philosophy should be one of judicial self-restraint, with rulings based on established case law precedent.

promises.text: Said in 2020 that he would uphold the Constitution and laws and ensure fair and equal access to justice for all.

record.text: Elected chief justice of the Ninth Court of Appeals without opposition in the 2020 general election and took office January 1, 2021.

notes.text: Texasjudges.org lists no opponent in the November 2026 general election.

candidates.current_role: U.S. Representative for Texas' 25th District since 2013
candidates.background: Roger Williams was raised in Fort Worth, attended Texas Christian University and played in the Atlanta Braves farm system. He runs a family-owned car dealership and cattle operation and coached baseball at TCU. He was first elected to Congress in 2012 and lives in Weatherford.

photo.credit: Official portrait, U.S. House of Representatives

priorities.text: Prioritizes lower taxes and federal spending cuts.
Prioritizes deregulation and help for small businesses.
Prioritizes border security and support for Israel.

record.text: Voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1), the 2025 budget reconciliation law that extended tax cuts and reduced projected federal Medicaid spending, on House passage in May 2025 and final passage in July 2025.
Did not vote on the Laken Riley Act (S. 5), which requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft-related or certain violent crimes, in January 2025.
Voted for the SAVE Act (H.R. 22), which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections, in April 2025.
Voted for the Protect Children's Innocence Act (H.R. 3492), which would make certain gender transition procedures on minors a federal crime, in December 2025.
Voted for the Do No Harm in Medicaid Act (H.R. 498), which would bar Medicaid funding for gender transition procedures for minors, in December 2025.
Voted against H.J.Res. 72, a resolution to end the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods, in February 2026.
Voted against H.R. 1834, which would extend expanded Affordable Care Act premium tax credits for three years and passed the House 230 to 196, in January 2026.
Voted for the Secure America Act (S. 2), which passed the House on a party-line vote, in June 2026.
Did not vote on the Born-Alive Abortion Survivors Protection Act (H.R. 21) in January 2025.
Introduced the Bulletproof Law Enforcement Vehicles Act to allow federal funds for police vehicle security upgrades.

q_tariffs.summary: Voted against ending the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods.

candidates.name: Keith Bell
candidates.current_role: Texas State Representative, District 4, since 2019
candidates.background: Keith Bell of Forney has represented House District 4 since 2019. He founded Intex Electrical Contractors in 1983, holds a master electrician license and served 20 years on the Forney ISD school board. He is a graduate of Dallas Baptist University.

photo.credit: Official portrait, Texas House of Representatives

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on its April 2025 House passage vote.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the House school finance and teacher pay bill.
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025), the final version of the school finance bill.
Was absent for the vote on SB 10 (2025), requiring display of the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), the constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent felony charges.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned consumable hemp-derived THC products (later vetoed by the governor).
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting purchases of Texas land by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversary nations.
Voted for SB 8 (2025, regular session), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Voted against Amendment No. 22 to the 2025 budget (SB 1), which directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; the amendment failed 63 to 85.
Voted for the 2026-27 state budget (SB 1) on House passage in April 2025.
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders.
Voted for HB 7 (2025, second called session), allowing civil lawsuits over the manufacture and distribution of abortion-inducing drugs.
In the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker, voted for Dustin Burrows, who was elected Speaker, over David Cook.
In April 2023 voted yes on the motion to table, and yes on adoption of, Amendment No. 45 to the budget, which barred state spending on vouchers or similar programs.
Voted for Amendment No. 2 to HB 1 (November 2023), which removed education savings accounts from the bill.
Voted for SB 14 (2023), prohibiting gender transition medical treatments for minors.
Voted for the 2023 motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2127, which limits city and county regulations in fields occupied by state law.
Voted for HR 2377 (May 2023), the articles of impeachment against Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was later acquitted by the Senate.
Voted for SB 3 (fourth called session, 2023), funding border barrier construction and border security operations.
Voted for SB 4 (fourth called session, 2023), creating a state criminal offense for illegal entry from a foreign nation.
Authored HB 12 (2025), on review and audit of state agency operations, and HB 120 (2025), on college, career and military readiness and career and technology education; both became law.
Authored HB 5033 (2025), relating to the state authority to run a vehicle emissions inspection program, which became law.
Filed HB 264 (2025) to dedicate certain surplus state revenue to property tax relief and HJR 36 to allow a lower homestead appraisal cap; neither passed.

notes.text: In a 2018 ATPE survey he answered "No!" when asked whether he would vote for any voucher or education savings account program; he voted for SB 2 in 2025.
Endorsed by Texas Parent PAC in the 2018 and 2022 general elections, according to ATPE.

candidates.current_role: Texas State Representative, District 18, since 2025
candidates.background: Janis Holt of Silsbee was elected to House District 18 in 2024. She and her husband own Hi-Tech Air Purification Systems and raise Angus cattle. She has worked as a dental assistant and fourth-grade teacher and has served on the Silsbee ISD board since 2014.

photo.credit: Official portrait, Texas House of Representatives

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on its April 2025 House passage vote.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the House school finance and teacher pay bill.
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025), the final version of the school finance bill.
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring display of the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), the constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent felony charges.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned consumable hemp-derived THC products (later vetoed by the governor).
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting purchases of Texas land by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversary nations.
Voted for SB 8 (2025, regular session), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Voted against Amendment No. 22 to the 2025 budget (SB 1), which directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; the amendment failed 63 to 85.
Voted against the 2026-27 state budget (SB 1) on House passage in April 2025.
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders.
Voted for HB 7 (2025, second called session), allowing civil lawsuits over the manufacture and distribution of abortion-inducing drugs.
In the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker, voted for David Cook over Dustin Burrows, who was elected Speaker.
Authored HJR 140 (2025), a constitutional amendment on the membership and authority of the State Commission on Judicial Conduct; it did not pass.

candidates.name: Drew Darby
candidates.current_role: State Representative, Texas House District 72, since 2007
candidates.background: Darby is a San Angelo native with a business degree in finance and a law degree from the University of Texas. He was first elected in 2006, serves on the Appropriations and Higher Education committees and ran unopposed in the 2026 Republican primary.

photo.credit: Official portrait, Texas House of Representatives

priorities.text: Campaign says West Texas should not be treated as a source of energy, food, tax dollars and water for larger cities to the east.
Told ATPE in 2024 his priorities were more school funding, higher teacher pay and school safety funding, resisting unfunded mandates and reforming testing.

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program; it passed the House 86 to 61.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the main public school finance bill, on third reading; it passed 142 to 5.
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025 school finance); it prevailed 122 to 13.
Voted against a 2025 budget amendment by Rep. John Bucy directing the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; it failed 63 to 85.
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting land purchases by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversary countries; it passed 86 to 59.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), a constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent offenses; it was adopted 133 to 8.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations; it passed 118 to 25.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned most consumable hemp-derived THC products, on second reading; it advanced 95 to 44.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), the hemp-derived THC products bill, on third reading; it passed 87 to 54.
Voted for SB 33 (2025), barring local governments from funding travel for abortion services; it passed 87 to 58.
Voted for SB 8 (2025), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement; it passed 86 to 47.
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms; it passed 82 to 46.
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting the recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders; it passed 86 to 53.
Voted for the conference report on SB 1, the 2026-2027 state budget; it was adopted 107 to 21.
Voted for HB 4 (2025 second called session), redrawing Texas congressional districts; it passed 88 to 52.
Voted for HB 7 (2025 second called session), restricting abortion-inducing drugs; it passed 82 to 48.
Voted for a 2023 budget amendment (Amendment No. 45 to HB 1) barring the use of state funds for school vouchers or similar programs; it was adopted 86 to 52.
Voted for the November 2023 amendment offered by Rep. John Raney, Rep. Drew Darby and others that struck the education savings account program from HB 1; it was adopted 84 to 63.
Voted for SB 14 (2023), banning gender transition medical treatments for minors; it passed 87 to 56.
Voted for HR 2377 (2023), impeaching Attorney General Ken Paxton; it was adopted 121 to 23.
Voted for SB 3 (2023 fourth called session), funding state border barrier construction; it passed 84 to 59.
Voted for SB 4 (2023 fourth called session), creating a state offense for illegal entry from a foreign nation; it passed 83 to 61.
Co-offered the November 2023 amendment that struck the education savings account program from HB 1.
Authored HB 48 (2025), creating an oilfield theft prevention unit at DPS, and HB 49 on treatment and reuse of oil and gas waste fluids, which became law.

notes.text: Endorsed by Texas Parent PAC in 2006, 2020 and 2022 and supported by the group in 2024, according to ATPE.
Opposed vouchers in 2023 votes and in his 2024 ATPE survey, then voted for SB 2 in 2025.

candidates.name: Angelia Orr
candidates.current_role: Texas State Representative, District 13, since 2023
candidates.background: Angelia Orr of Hill County has represented House District 13 since 2023. She is a small business owner, former substitute teacher and former Itasca ISD trustee, and she served as Hill County district clerk. She graduated from Texas A&M University in 1992.

photo.credit: Official portrait, Texas House of Representatives

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on its April 2025 House passage vote.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the House school finance and teacher pay bill.

Was absent for the vote on the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025), the final version of the school finance bill; a statement of vote in the journal says the member would have voted yes.
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring display of the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), the constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent felony charges.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned consumable hemp-derived THC products (later vetoed by the governor).
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting purchases of Texas land by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversary nations.
Voted for SB 8 (2025, regular session), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Voted against Amendment No. 22 to the 2025 budget (SB 1), which directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; the amendment failed 63 to 85.
Voted for the 2026-27 state budget (SB 1) on House passage in April 2025.
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders.
Voted for HB 7 (2025, second called session), allowing civil lawsuits over the manufacture and distribution of abortion-inducing drugs.
In the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker, voted for Dustin Burrows, who was elected Speaker, over David Cook.
In April 2023 voted yes on the motion to table, and yes on adoption of, Amendment No. 45 to the budget, which barred state spending on vouchers or similar programs.
Voted against Amendment No. 2 to HB 1 (November 2023), which removed education savings accounts from the bill.
Voted for SB 14 (2023), prohibiting gender transition medical treatments for minors.
Voted for the 2023 motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2127, which limits city and county regulations in fields occupied by state law.
Voted for HR 2377 (May 2023), the articles of impeachment against Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was later acquitted by the Senate.
Voted for SB 3 (fourth called session, 2023), funding border barrier construction and border security operations.
Voted for SB 4 (fourth called session, 2023), creating a state criminal offense for illegal entry from a foreign nation.
Authored HB 24 (2025), on procedures for zoning changes, and HB 128 (2025), on sister-city agreements with foreign countries; both became law.
Authored HB 3801 (2025), creating the Health Professions Workforce Coordinating Council, which became law.

notes.text: In a 2022 ATPE survey she wrote that she was against any type of voucher program; she later voted for voucher legislation in 2023 and 2025.
The Waco Tribune-Herald editorial board urged voters to oppose her in the 2024 primary, citing the change in her voucher position, and Gov. Greg Abbott endorsed her, according to ATPE.

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program; it passed the House 86 to 61.

candidates.name: Wes Virdell
candidates.current_role: State Representative, Texas House District 53, since 2025
candidates.background: Virdell represents a district that includes Medina County. He was first elected in 2024 and ran unopposed in the 2026 Republican primary.

photo.credit: Official portrait, Texas House of Representatives

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program; it passed the House 86 to 61.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the main public school finance bill, on third reading; it passed 142 to 5.
Voted against a 2025 budget amendment by Rep. John Bucy directing the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; it failed 63 to 85.
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting land purchases by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversary countries; it passed 86 to 59.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), a constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent offenses; it was adopted 133 to 8.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations; it passed 118 to 25.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned most consumable hemp-derived THC products, on second reading; it advanced 95 to 44.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), the hemp-derived THC products bill, on third reading; it passed 87 to 54.
Voted for SB 33 (2025), barring local governments from funding travel for abortion services; it passed 87 to 58.
Voted for SB 8 (2025), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement; it passed 86 to 47.
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms; it passed 82 to 46.
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting the recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders; it passed 86 to 53.
Voted against the conference report on SB 1, the 2026-2027 state budget; it was adopted 107 to 21.
Voted for HB 4 (2025 second called session), redrawing Texas congressional districts; it passed 88 to 52.
Voted for HB 7 (2025 second called session), restricting abortion-inducing drugs; it passed 82 to 48.
Authored HB 3053 (2025) on municipal and county firearm buyback programs, which became law.

Authored HJR 116 (2025) on limiting federal authority to regulate firearms in Texas, HB 2470 on the age to carry a handgun and HB 1923 removing fingerprint requirements for handgun licenses; none passed.

candidates.name: Kevin Sparks
candidates.current_role: Texas State Senator, District 31, since 2023
candidates.background: Sparks is a Midland oil and gas operator who started at his family's company, Discovery Operating, as a pumper and roustabout and later became chief executive. He earned a business degree from the University of Texas at Austin in 1985 and is a former Texas Public Policy Foundation board member. He was elected to the Senate in 2022.

priorities.text: Focuses on grid reliability, including investing in dispatchable natural gas and reforming the Texas Energy Fund.
Seeks water infrastructure cybersecurity, rural access to water programs and better water resource management.
Calls for fully funding state troopers and the National Guard for border security and opposes sanctuary city policies.
Cites foster care reform and combating oilfield theft as legislative priorities.
Supports lower taxes, fewer regulations and less spending.

promises.text: Urges the PUC to defer further 765-kV transmission decisions until the 90th Legislature reviews costs and alternatives.

record.text: Filed SB 714 (2025) to offset market effects of federal renewable energy subsidies and SB 970 to prioritize baseload generation in the Texas Energy Fund.
Coauthored SB 2 (2025) and voted for it.
Joint author of and voted for SB 10 (2025), SB 13 (2025) and SB 17 (2025).
Coauthored and voted for SB 3 (2025), the hemp-derived THC ban that was vetoed.
Joint author of SB 819 (2025) on renewable energy facilities and voted for SB 388 (2025) on dispatchable generation goals.
Joint author of SB 16 (2025) on proof of citizenship and coauthor of SB 12 (2025).
Voted for SB 14 (2023) and coauthored SB 4 (2023, 4th called session) on illegal entry.

q_fossil_priority.summary: Says dispatchable natural gas should be prioritized and federal renewable subsidies distort the market.

q_border_state.summary: His campaign issues page calls for fully funding State Troopers and the Texas National Guard and demands federal reimbursement for Texas border security spending.

q_ten_commandments.summary: Joint author of and voted for SB 10 (2025).

q_cannabis.summary: Coauthored SB 3 (2025).

q_bail.summary: Coauthored SJR 5 (2025).

q_trans_minors.summary: Coauthored and voted for SB 14 (2023).

q_voting_access.summary: Joint author of SB 16 (2025); supports photo ID to vote.

q_abortion.summary: His campaign issues page says "we must always protect innocent life, born and unborn" and that tax dollars should never fund any entity involved with abortion.

q_water.summary: Joint author of SB 7 (2025), which he backed as dedicating significant funding to water.

q_preemption.summary: Voted for HB 2127 (2023).

candidates.background: Craddick, of Midland, was first elected to the House in 1968 and is its longest-serving member. He served as Speaker of the House from 2003 to 2009. His campaign says he chairs the House Transportation Committee; he holds BBA and MBA degrees from Texas Tech University.

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created a $1 billion education savings account program for private school and homeschool costs; it passed the House 86 to 61.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the school finance and teacher pay bill, on House passage (142 to 5).
Voted against Amendment No. 22 to the 2026-2027 budget (April 2025), which would have directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; it failed 63 to 85.
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting land purchases by people and entities tied to designated foreign adversary countries; it passed 86 to 59.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), a proposed constitutional amendment expanding when bail can be denied for certain violent or sexual offenses (adopted 133 to 8).
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail and pretrial release procedures (passed 118 to 25).
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned most consumable hemp-derived THC products; it passed the House 87 to 54.
Voted for SB 8 (2025), requiring agreements between county sheriffs and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to enforce federal immigration law (passed 86 to 47).
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms (passed 82 to 46).
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders (passed 86 to 53).
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HJR 7 (2025), a constitutional amendment dedicating sales tax revenue to the Texas water fund (122 to 12).
Voted for SB 33 (2025), barring local governments from funding travel for abortions (passed 87 to 58).
Voted for HB 4 (2025, second called session), redrawing Texas congressional districts (passed 88 to 52).
Voted for HB 7 (2025, second called session), prohibiting the manufacture and provision of abortion-inducing drugs and authorizing private lawsuits (passed 82 to 48).
Voted for SB 14 (2023), banning gender transition medical treatments for minors (passed 87 to 56).
Voted against the May 2023 resolution impeaching Attorney General Ken Paxton (adopted 121 to 23).
Voted against Amendment No. 45 to the 2023 House budget, barring state money for vouchers or education savings accounts (adopted 86 to 52).
Voted against the November 2023 amendment removing the education savings account program from HB 1 (adopted 84 to 63).
Voted for SB 3 (2023, fourth called session), funding border barrier construction and border security operations (passed 84 to 59).
Voted for SB 4 (2023, fourth called session), creating a state offense for illegal entry (passed 83 to 61).
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2127 (2023), which preempts certain city and county regulation (84 to 58).
Authored HB 5 and HJR 3 (2025), to create the Dementia Prevention and Research Institute of Texas; both were left pending in committee.
Authored HB 3707 (2025) on oil and gas equipment and waste theft and HB 5453 (2025) on transportation project funding.

notes.text: Was one of 23 House members who voted against impeaching Attorney General Ken Paxton in May 2023.

candidates.name: Will Metcalf
candidates.current_role: Texas State Representative, District 16, since 2015
candidates.background: Will Metcalf is a sixth-generation Montgomery County resident who has represented House District 16 since 2015. He works in banking as vice president and director of business development at Spirit of Texas Bank and manages real estate investments. He holds a criminal justice degree from Sam Houston State University.

photo.credit: Official portrait, Texas House of Representatives

priorities.text: Calls property tax relief and long-term predictability for homeowners and businesses crucial priorities.
Wants every child to have a high-quality education, fairly paid teachers and less high-stakes testing.
Names infrastructure such as transportation and water, and protecting conservative family values, as the biggest challenges.

promises.text: Says he would lower appraisal caps, raise the state share of school funding and fully eliminate school maintenance and operations property taxes.

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on its April 2025 House passage vote.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the House school finance and teacher pay bill.
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025), the final version of the school finance bill.
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring display of the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), the constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent felony charges.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned consumable hemp-derived THC products (later vetoed by the governor).
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting purchases of Texas land by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversary nations.
Voted for SB 8 (2025, regular session), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Voted against Amendment No. 22 to the 2025 budget (SB 1), which directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; the amendment failed 63 to 85.
Voted for the 2026-27 state budget (SB 1) on House passage in April 2025.
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders.
Voted for HB 7 (2025, second called session), allowing civil lawsuits over the manufacture and distribution of abortion-inducing drugs.
In the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker, voted for Dustin Burrows, who was elected Speaker, over David Cook.
In April 2023 voted yes on the motion to table, and no on adoption of, Amendment No. 45 to the budget, which barred state spending on vouchers or similar programs.
Voted against Amendment No. 2 to HB 1 (November 2023), which removed education savings accounts from the bill.
Voted for SB 14 (2023), prohibiting gender transition medical treatments for minors.
Voted for the 2023 motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2127, which limits city and county regulations in fields occupied by state law.
Voted for HR 2377 (May 2023), the articles of impeachment against Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was later acquitted by the Senate.
Voted for SB 3 (fourth called session, 2023), funding border barrier construction and border security operations.
Voted for SB 4 (fourth called session, 2023), creating a state criminal offense for illegal entry from a foreign nation.
Authored HB 34 (2025), prohibiting state investment in certain countries, and HB 1458 (2025), on armed security officers at public schools; both became law.
Filed HB 356 and HJR 39 (2025) to allow a lower homestead appraisal cap; neither passed.

notes.text: Defeated Jon Bouche in the March 2026 Republican primary.

candidates.name: Todd Hunter
candidates.current_role: Texas State Representative, District 32; chair of the House Calendars Committee
candidates.background: Todd Hunter has practiced law in Corpus Christi since 1978. He served four House terms after his first election in 1988 and returned to the House in 2008, and he was sworn in for his thirteenth term in 2025. He chaired the State Affairs Committee in 2023 and the Calendars Committee in 2025.

photo.credit: Official portrait, Texas House of Representatives

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on its April 2025 House passage vote.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the House school finance and teacher pay bill.
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025), the final version of the school finance bill.
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring display of the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), the constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent felony charges.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned consumable hemp-derived THC products (later vetoed by the governor).
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting purchases of Texas land by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversary nations.
Voted for SB 8 (2025, regular session), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Voted against Amendment No. 22 to the 2025 budget (SB 1), which directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; the amendment failed 63 to 85.
Voted for the 2026-27 state budget (SB 1) on House passage in April 2025.
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders.
Voted for HB 7 (2025, second called session), allowing civil lawsuits over the manufacture and distribution of abortion-inducing drugs.
In the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker, voted for Dustin Burrows, who was elected Speaker, over David Cook.
In April 2023 voted yes on the motion to table, and no on adoption of, Amendment No. 45 to the budget, which barred state spending on vouchers or similar programs.
Voted against Amendment No. 2 to HB 1 (November 2023), which removed education savings accounts from the bill.
Voted for SB 14 (2023), prohibiting gender transition medical treatments for minors.
Voted for the 2023 motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2127, which limits city and county regulations in fields occupied by state law.
Voted for HR 2377 (May 2023), the articles of impeachment against Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was later acquitted by the Senate.
Voted for SB 3 (fourth called session, 2023), funding border barrier construction and border security operations.
Voted for SB 4 (fourth called session, 2023), creating a state criminal offense for illegal entry from a foreign nation.
Authored HB 3689 (2025), on funding losses and operating expenses of the Texas Windstorm Insurance Association, and HB 4215 (2025), regulating delivery network companies; both became law.

notes.text: Gov. Greg Abbott endorsed him in the 2024 Republican primary, according to ATPE. He has not responded to recent ATPE surveys.

candidates.name: Craig Goldman
candidates.current_role: U.S. Representative for Texas' 12th District since 2025
candidates.background: Craig Goldman is a Fort Worth native with a degree from the University of Texas at Austin. He worked at his family's gourmet food and wine store. He served 12 years in the Texas House, where he chaired the Energy Resources Committee, before his election to Congress in 2024.

photo.credit: Official portrait, U.S. House of Representatives (Office of the Clerk)

priorities.text: Prioritizes border security and the American taxpayer.
Prioritizes reducing taxes and strengthening national defense.
Pledges to fiercely protect Second Amendment rights.

record.text: Voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1), the 2025 budget reconciliation law that extended tax cuts and reduced projected federal Medicaid spending, on House passage in May 2025 and final passage in July 2025.
Voted for the Laken Riley Act (S. 5), which requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft-related or certain violent crimes, in January 2025.
Voted for the SAVE Act (H.R. 22), which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections, in April 2025.
Voted for the Protect Children's Innocence Act (H.R. 3492), which would make certain gender transition procedures on minors a federal crime, in December 2025.
Voted for the Do No Harm in Medicaid Act (H.R. 498), which would bar Medicaid funding for gender transition procedures for minors, in December 2025.
Voted against H.J.Res. 72, a resolution to end the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods, in February 2026.
Voted against H.R. 1834, which would extend expanded Affordable Care Act premium tax credits for three years and passed the House 230 to 196, in January 2026.
Voted for the Secure America Act (S. 2), which passed the House on a party-line vote, in June 2026.
Voted for the Born-Alive Abortion Survivors Protection Act (H.R. 21) in January 2025.
As a state representative, authored House Bill 6 in 2023, creating a criminal offense for fentanyl-related deaths, according to his campaign.
Introduced the Better Care, Better Cost Act on Medicaid managed care incentives and the Abraham Accords Expansion Act of 2026.
Says he passed what he calls the strongest election integrity bill in Texas history as a state representative.

q_federal_spending.summary: Voted for the 2025 reconciliation law, which reduced projected federal Medicaid spending.

q_voting_access.summary: Passed a Texas election bill targeting ballot harvesting and voted for the SAVE Act.

q_trans_minors.summary: Voted in the Texas House to ban gender transition surgeries on minors and voted for federal bills restricting such treatments.

q_tariffs.summary: Voted against ending the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods.

q_border_state.summary: Says he voted in the Texas House for record border security funding and the use of the National Guard.

q_abortion.summary: Supported the Texas Heartbeat bill and voted to defund abortion providers as a state representative.

q_gun_laws.summary: Says he will fiercely protect Second Amendment rights and is endorsed by the NRA.

candidates.name: Mike Olcott
candidates.current_role: State Representative, Texas House District 60, since 2025
candidates.background: Olcott represents a district that includes Parker County. He defeated then-Rep. Glenn Rogers in the 2024 Republican primary after losing to him in 2022, and won the 2026 Republican primary.

photo.credit: Official portrait, Texas House of Representatives

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program; it passed the House 86 to 61.
Voted against HB 2 (2025), the main public school finance bill, on third reading; it passed 142 to 5.
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025 school finance); it prevailed 122 to 13.
Voted against a 2025 budget amendment by Rep. John Bucy directing the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; it failed 63 to 85.
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting land purchases by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversary countries; it passed 86 to 59.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), a constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent offenses; it was adopted 133 to 8.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations; it passed 118 to 25.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned most consumable hemp-derived THC products, on second reading; it advanced 95 to 44.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), the hemp-derived THC products bill, on third reading; it passed 87 to 54.
Voted for SB 33 (2025), barring local governments from funding travel for abortion services; it passed 87 to 58.
Voted for SB 8 (2025), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement; it passed 86 to 47.
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms; it passed 82 to 46.
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting the recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders; it passed 86 to 53.
Voted against the conference report on SB 1, the 2026-2027 state budget; it was adopted 107 to 21.
Voted for HB 4 (2025 second called session), redrawing Texas congressional districts; it passed 88 to 52.

candidates.name: Caroline Fairly
candidates.current_role: State Representative, Texas House District 87, since 2025
candidates.background: Fairly is an Amarillo native and a graduate of Abilene Christian University, where she studied business marketing. She worked on Ronny Jackson's congressional campaign and on his congressional staff, then worked as a medical negotiator at The OccuNet Company. She was first elected in 2024.

photo.credit: Official portrait, Texas House of Representatives

priorities.text: Her House biography says she worked on health care policy, digital safety legislation, water resources, and phone-free learning in schools in her first session.
Campaigns on faith, family, and conservative leadership.

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created a $1 billion education savings account program for private school and homeschool costs; it passed the House 86 to 61.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the school finance and teacher pay bill, on House passage (142 to 5).
Voted against Amendment No. 22 to the 2026-2027 budget (April 2025), which would have directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; it failed 63 to 85.
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting land purchases by people and entities tied to designated foreign adversary countries; it passed 86 to 59.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), a proposed constitutional amendment expanding when bail can be denied for certain violent or sexual offenses (adopted 133 to 8).
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail and pretrial release procedures (passed 118 to 25).
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned most consumable hemp-derived THC products; it passed the House 87 to 54.
Was recorded absent for the vote on SB 8 (2025), requiring agreements between county sheriffs and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to enforce federal immigration law (passed 86 to 47).
Was recorded absent for the vote on SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms (passed 82 to 46).
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders (passed 86 to 53).
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HJR 7 (2025), a constitutional amendment dedicating sales tax revenue to the Texas water fund (122 to 12).
Voted for SB 33 (2025), barring local governments from funding travel for abortions (passed 87 to 58).
Voted for HB 4 (2025, second called session), redrawing Texas congressional districts (passed 88 to 52).
Voted for HB 7 (2025, second called session), prohibiting the manufacture and provision of abortion-inducing drugs and authorizing private lawsuits (passed 82 to 48).
Authored HB 1481 (2025), requiring school policies on student use of personal communication devices, and HB 1700 (2025) on telehealth records; both became law.

notes.text: Endorsed by Gov. Greg Abbott in the 2024 Republican primary, according to ATPE.
Did not respond to the 2024 or 2026 ATPE candidate surveys.

candidates.name: Tim O'Hare
candidates.current_role: Tarrant County Judge since 2023
candidates.background: O'Hare has been Tarrant County Judge since January 2023. He earned a BBA in finance from the University of Texas at Austin and a law degree from SMU, and ran a law firm and real estate investment company for more than 25 years. He served on the Farmers Branch City Council and as mayor from 2008 to 2011, and was chairman of the Tarrant County Republican Party. He lives in Southlake.

priorities.text: Campaigns on lower taxes and less spending, citing what he calls the largest property tax cuts in county history.
Says he wants to make Tarrant County the safest large county in Texas and has increased funding for law enforcement.
Highlights election changes he championed, including numbered paper ballots and ending internet-based transmission of results.
Says he wants to keep property taxes down and attract more corporate relocations.

record.text: Under O'Hare the county adopted the maximum 20% homestead exemption for the first time; he says it saves homeowners $262 million.

In September 2025 the court adopted a county tax rate of 18.62 cents per $100 valuation, below the no-new-revenue rate, after an earlier vote was blocked when two Democratic commissioners were absent.
Says the county operating budget fell by $81 million over three years while funding for the sheriff and district attorney rose.
Pushed the 2025 mid-decade redistricting of commissioner precincts, adopted 3 to 2.
In December 2024 the court passed a resolution asking the Legislature to fund a mental health hospital for Tarrant County.
Proposed a September 2025 budget amendment cutting the two Democratic commissioners' staffs and travel budgets; it was reversed after the tax rate passed.

notes.text: Ballotpedia lists endorsements from Gov. Greg Abbott, Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, Sen. Ted Cruz, Texas Right to Life, Texas Values Action and Young Conservatives of Texas, among others.

q_county_tax.summary: Has led the court in adopting tax rates below the no-new-revenue rate and the maximum homestead exemption, and says he wants to keep property taxes down.

issue_notes.summary: Says public safety is the foundation for job growth and that detention officers received record raises two years in a row.

candidates.name: Brooks Landgraf
candidates.current_role: State Representative, Texas House District 81, since 2015
candidates.background: Landgraf is an Odessa attorney from a West Texas ranching family who represents Ector, Loving, Ward, and Winkler counties. He graduated from Texas A&M University and St. Mary's University School of Law. His House biography says he chairs the House Environmental Regulation Committee.

photo.credit: Official portrait, Texas House of Representatives

priorities.text: His House biography lists protecting the Permian Basin energy economy, strengthening infrastructure, defending individual liberties, promoting life, and keeping Texas affordable.

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created a $1 billion education savings account program for private school and homeschool costs; it passed the House 86 to 61.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the school finance and teacher pay bill, on House passage (142 to 5).
Voted against Amendment No. 22 to the 2026-2027 budget (April 2025), which would have directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; it failed 63 to 85.
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting land purchases by people and entities tied to designated foreign adversary countries; it passed 86 to 59.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), a proposed constitutional amendment expanding when bail can be denied for certain violent or sexual offenses (adopted 133 to 8).
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail and pretrial release procedures (passed 118 to 25).
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned most consumable hemp-derived THC products; it passed the House 87 to 54.
Voted for SB 8 (2025), requiring agreements between county sheriffs and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to enforce federal immigration law (passed 86 to 47).
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms (passed 82 to 46).
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders (passed 86 to 53).
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HJR 7 (2025), a constitutional amendment dedicating sales tax revenue to the Texas water fund (122 to 12).
Voted for SB 33 (2025), barring local governments from funding travel for abortions (passed 87 to 58).
Voted for HB 4 (2025, second called session), redrawing Texas congressional districts (passed 88 to 52).
Voted for HB 7 (2025, second called session), prohibiting the manufacture and provision of abortion-inducing drugs and authorizing private lawsuits (passed 82 to 48).
Voted for SB 14 (2023), banning gender transition medical treatments for minors (passed 87 to 56).
Voted for the May 2023 resolution impeaching Attorney General Ken Paxton (adopted 121 to 23).
Voted for Amendment No. 45 to the 2023 House budget, barring state money for vouchers or education savings accounts (adopted 86 to 52).
Voted against the November 2023 amendment removing the education savings account program from HB 1 (adopted 84 to 63).
Voted for SB 3 (2023, fourth called session), funding border barrier construction and border security operations (passed 84 to 59).
Voted for SB 4 (2023, fourth called session), creating a state offense for illegal entry (passed 83 to 61).
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2127 (2023), which preempts certain city and county regulation (84 to 58).

Authored HB 40 (2025) on the business court, HB 4112 (2025) on disposal or storage of high-level radioactive waste, and HB 5342 (2025) on behavioral health crisis services and the 988 line; all became law.
Authored HB 1808 (2025) on regulation of produced water from oil and gas operations; it was referred to committee.

notes.text: Endorsed by Gov. Greg Abbott in the 2024 Republican primary, according to ATPE.
Did not respond to the 2026 ATPE candidate survey.

candidates.name: Greg Casar
candidates.current_role: U.S. Representative for Texas' 35th District since 2023
candidates.background: Greg Casar is a native Texan and son of Mexican immigrants who graduated from the University of Virginia. He worked as a labor organizer and policy director at the Workers Defense Project and served on the Austin City Council from 2015 to 2022. He was elected to Congress in 2022 and is running in the redrawn 37th District. He lives in Austin with his spouse, Asha.

photo.credit: Official portrait, U.S. House of Representatives

priorities.text: Campaigns on good jobs, reproductive rights, Medicare for All and ending the climate crisis.
Supports federal legislation to end partisan gerrymandering and restore the Voting Rights Act.
Supports ending the filibuster and expanding the U.S. Supreme Court.
Does not accept corporate PAC donations and supports overturning Citizens United.

record.text: Voted against the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1), the 2025 budget reconciliation law that extended tax cuts and reduced projected federal Medicaid spending, on House passage in May 2025 and final passage in July 2025.
Voted against the Laken Riley Act (S. 5), which requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft-related or certain violent crimes, in January 2025.
Voted against the SAVE Act (H.R. 22), which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections, in April 2025.
Voted against the Protect Children's Innocence Act (H.R. 3492), which would make certain gender transition procedures on minors a federal crime, in December 2025.
Did not vote on the Do No Harm in Medicaid Act (H.R. 498), which would bar Medicaid funding for gender transition procedures for minors, in December 2025.
Voted for H.J.Res. 72, a resolution to end the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods, in February 2026.
Voted for H.R. 1834, which would extend expanded Affordable Care Act premium tax credits for three years and passed the House 230 to 196, in January 2026.
Voted against the Secure America Act (S. 2), which passed the House on a party-line vote, in June 2026.
Voted against the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (H.R. 7148) in January 2026.
Introduced the Double the Wage for Overtime Act.
As an Austin City Council member, ended arrests and citations for personal marijuana use in Austin, according to his campaign.
Co-leads the New Way Forward Act and cosponsors the Women's Health Protection Act and the Assault Weapons Ban.

q_federal_spending.summary: Voted against the 2025 reconciliation law, which reduced projected federal Medicaid spending.

q_voting_access.summary: Cosponsors the Freedom to Vote Act, which would establish automatic voter registration.

q_trans_minors.summary: Voted against a bill to make certain gender transition procedures on minors a federal crime.

q_tariffs.summary: Voted for a resolution to end the national emergency used to impose tariffs on Canadian goods.

q_cannabis.summary: Supports legalizing marijuana and expunging past records.

q_abortion.summary: Supports making Roe v. Wade federal law and cosponsors the Women's Health Protection Act.

q_gun_laws.summary: Supports universal background checks, ending permitless carry and banning assault weapons.

q_legal_status.summary: Supports the American Dream and Promise Act and related bills offering legal status to immigrants.

q_deportation.summary: Says immigrant families deserve to live free from fear of separation and deportation.

q_border_state.summary: Co-leads a bill he says would roll back Gov. Abbott's militarization of the border.

q_medicaid.summary: Cosponsors Medicare for All, which goes beyond Medicaid expansion.

q_fossil_priority.summary: Supports the Green New Deal and union jobs in clean energy.

q_min_wage.summary: Led efforts on the Austin City Council to raise the minimum wage, according to his campaign.

candidates.name: Aj Louderback
candidates.current_role: Texas State Representative, District 30, since 2025
candidates.background: AJ Louderback was elected to House District 30 in 2024 and serves in the 89th Legislature.

photo.credit: Official portrait, Texas House of Representatives

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on its April 2025 House passage vote.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the House school finance and teacher pay bill.
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025), the final version of the school finance bill.
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring display of the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), the constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent felony charges.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned consumable hemp-derived THC products (later vetoed by the governor).
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting purchases of Texas land by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversary nations.
Voted for SB 8 (2025, regular session), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Voted against Amendment No. 22 to the 2025 budget (SB 1), which directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; the amendment failed 63 to 85.
Voted for the 2026-27 state budget (SB 1) on House passage in April 2025.
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders.
Voted for HB 7 (2025, second called session), allowing civil lawsuits over the manufacture and distribution of abortion-inducing drugs.
In the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker, voted for David Cook over Dustin Burrows, who was elected Speaker.
Authored HB 2257 (2025), requiring county sheriffs to enter agreements with the federal government to enforce immigration law; it did not pass, and the House later passed the similar SB 8.
Authored HB 3778 (2025), on using geothermal energy as a dispatchable generation resource, and HB 1487 (2025), removing the fee for a license to carry a handgun; neither became law.
Authored HB 2820 (2025), on charitable bingo operating capital, which became law.

q_vouchers.summary: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program.

q_school_funding.summary: Voted for HB 2 (2025), the school finance and teacher pay bill, on House passage and final concurrence.

q_ten_commandments.summary: Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays in classrooms.

q_medicaid.summary: Voted against a 2025 budget amendment directing the state to seek a waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility.

q_bail.summary: Voted for SJR 5 and SB 9 (2025), which expand denial of bail and tighten bail procedures for violent felony charges.

q_cannabis.summary: Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned consumable hemp-derived THC products.

q_foreign_land.summary: Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting land purchases by people and entities tied to foreign adversary nations.

q_deportation.summary: Authored HB 2257 (2025) requiring sheriff immigration enforcement agreements and voted for SB 8 (2025) on the same subject.

q_gun_laws.summary: Voted for SB 1362 (2025), which bars recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective (red flag) orders.

q_abortion.summary: Voted for HB 7 (2025), allowing civil suits over the distribution of abortion-inducing drugs.

candidates.current_role: State Representative, Texas House District 42 (Laredo); served 1993 to 1999 and since 2001
candidates.background: Raymond represents a Webb County district in Laredo. He was first elected in 1992, served through 1998, ran unsuccessfully for statewide office in 1998 and returned to the House after the 2000 election. He ran unopposed in the 2026 Democratic primary.

priorities.text: Campaigns on education, including better teacher pay and increased school funding.
Campaigns on expanding access to affordable health care.

Lists public safety with accountability in law enforcement as a priority.

record.text: Voted against SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program; it passed the House 86 to 61.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the main public school finance bill, on third reading; it passed 142 to 5.
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025 school finance); it prevailed 122 to 13.

Voted for SJR 5 (2025), a constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent offenses; it was adopted 133 to 8.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations; it passed 118 to 25.
Voted against SB 3 (2025), which would have banned most consumable hemp-derived THC products, on second reading; it advanced 95 to 44.
Voted against SB 3 (2025), the hemp-derived THC products bill, on third reading; it passed 87 to 54.
Voted for SB 33 (2025), barring local governments from funding travel for abortion services; it passed 87 to 58.
Voted for SB 8 (2025), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement; it passed 86 to 47.

Voted against HB 7 (2025 second called session), restricting abortion-inducing drugs; it passed 82 to 48.

candidates.background: McLaughlin served as mayor of Uvalde from 2014 until he resigned in 2023 to run for the House, and was mayor during the 2022 Robb Elementary School shooting. He won House District 80 in 2024. The district covers part of Webb County and several South Texas counties.

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created a $1 billion education savings account program for private school and homeschool costs; it passed the House 86 to 61.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the school finance and teacher pay bill, on House passage (142 to 5).
Voted against Amendment No. 22 to the 2026-2027 budget (April 2025), which would have directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; it failed 63 to 85.
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting land purchases by people and entities tied to designated foreign adversary countries; it passed 86 to 59.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), a proposed constitutional amendment expanding when bail can be denied for certain violent or sexual offenses (adopted 133 to 8).
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail and pretrial release procedures (passed 118 to 25).
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned most consumable hemp-derived THC products; it passed the House 87 to 54.
Voted for SB 8 (2025), requiring agreements between county sheriffs and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to enforce federal immigration law (passed 86 to 47).
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms (passed 82 to 46).
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders (passed 86 to 53).
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HJR 7 (2025), a constitutional amendment dedicating sales tax revenue to the Texas water fund (122 to 12).
Voted for SB 33 (2025), barring local governments from funding travel for abortions (passed 87 to 58).
Voted for HB 4 (2025, second called session), redrawing Texas congressional districts (passed 88 to 52).
Voted for HB 7 (2025, second called session), prohibiting the manufacture and provision of abortion-inducing drugs and authorizing private lawsuits (passed 82 to 48).
Authored HB 33 (2025), on active shooter incidents at schools and other emergencies, which became law.
Authored HB 3278 (2025), on a study of and incentives for solar and wind energy, which failed in committee, and HB 3587 (2025) on firearm safety instruction in schools.

notes.text: Won the 2024 general election with 59.5 percent of the vote over Cecilia Castellano, a seat previously held by a Democrat.

candidates.current_role: Texas State Representative, District 20
candidates.background: Terry Wilson of Georgetown is a retired U.S. Army colonel with more than 30 years of service and a former Department of Defense acquisition executive. He holds a business degree from Texas A&M University and a master's degree from the Air War College system.

photo.credit: Official portrait, Texas House of Representatives

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on its April 2025 House passage vote.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the House school finance and teacher pay bill.
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025), the final version of the school finance bill.
Voted for SB 10 (2025), requiring display of the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), the constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent felony charges.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned consumable hemp-derived THC products (later vetoed by the governor).
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting purchases of Texas land by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversary nations.
Voted for SB 8 (2025, regular session), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Voted against Amendment No. 22 to the 2025 budget (SB 1), which directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; the amendment failed 63 to 85.
Voted for the 2026-27 state budget (SB 1) on House passage in April 2025.
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders.
Voted for HB 7 (2025, second called session), allowing civil lawsuits over the manufacture and distribution of abortion-inducing drugs.
In the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker, voted for Dustin Burrows, who was elected Speaker, over David Cook.
In April 2023 voted yes on the motion to table, and no on adoption of, Amendment No. 45 to the budget, which barred state spending on vouchers or similar programs.
Voted against Amendment No. 2 to HB 1 (November 2023), which removed education savings accounts from the bill.
Voted for SB 14 (2023), prohibiting gender transition medical treatments for minors.
Voted for the 2023 motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2127, which limits city and county regulations in fields occupied by state law.
Voted for HR 2377 (May 2023), the articles of impeachment against Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was later acquitted by the Senate.
Voted for SB 3 (fourth called session, 2023), funding border barrier construction and border security operations.
Voted for SB 4 (fourth called session, 2023), creating a state criminal offense for illegal entry from a foreign nation.
Authored HB 127 (2025), on protecting universities from foreign adversaries and prosecuting trade secret theft, which became law.
Authored HB 5629 (2025), on occupational licensing for service members, veterans and military spouses, and HB 300 (2025), on the Texas Armed Services Scholarship Program; both became law.

candidates.name: John H. Bucy, III
candidates.current_role: State Representative, Texas House District 136, since 2019
candidates.background: Bucy is a small business owner whose organization runs athletic, academic and arts competitions for public school students. He represents parts of Williamson County, including Northwest Austin, Cedar Park and Round Rock. He was vice chair of the House Elections Committee in the 89th Legislature and holds a degree from Austin College.

photo.credit: Official portrait, Texas House of Representatives

priorities.text: Campaigns on strong public schools, access to health care, good jobs, equality and the freedom to vote.

record.text: Offered the 2025 budget amendment directing HHSC to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid, which failed 63 to 85.

In 2025 authored HB 197, HB 262 and HJR 21 (Medicaid expansion), HB 417 and HB 1917 (mail voting for any qualified voter), HB 311 (electronic voter registration), HB 454 (abolishing the death penalty) and HB 2975 (regulating cannabis); none became law.
Voted against SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on third reading.
In 2023 voted for the April 2023 budget amendment barring state funds for vouchers and for the November 2023 amendment removing education savings accounts from HB 1.
Voted for HB 2 (2025 school finance) on third reading and voted to concur in the final Senate version.
Voted for a 2025 budget amendment (Amendment No. 22 to SB 1) directing the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid, which failed 63 to 85.
Voted against SB 10 (2025), requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms.
Voted for SJR 5 (the 2025 bail constitutional amendment) and voted against SB 9 (2025 bail procedures).
Voted against SB 3 (2025), which would have banned most hemp-derived THC products, on third reading.

In 2025 voted against SB 17 (land purchases tied to designated foreign adversaries), SB 8 (requiring certain sheriffs to enter agreements with ICE) and SB 1362 (barring enforcement of extreme risk protective orders).
In the August 2025 second special session voted against HB 4 (2025 mid-decade congressional redistricting) and against HB 7 (2025, civil lawsuits over abortion-inducing drugs).

In 2023 voted against SB 14 (ban on gender transition treatments for minors), HB 2127 (state preemption of local regulations), SB 3 (state border barrier funding) and SB 4 (state illegal entry offense).
Voted for impeaching Attorney General Ken Paxton in May 2023.
Voted for Dustin Burrows over David Cook in the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker of the House.
Was recorded absent on August 5, 2025, when the House lacked a quorum during the House Democrats' walkout over congressional redistricting.

notes.text: Ran unopposed in the 2026 Democratic primary, according to ATPE.
Endorsed by Texas Parent PAC in 2018, 2020 and 2022, according to ATPE.

candidates.name: Steve Snell
candidates.current_role: Williamson County Judge since April 2025 (appointed)
candidates.background: Steve Snell was appointed Williamson County judge by the Commissioners Court on a 3-1 vote in March 2025 after Bill Gravell resigned. He spent about three decades in public schools, including six years as Liberty Hill ISD superintendent, and previously led Spring Hill ISD and was an assistant superintendent in Hutto ISD. He holds bachelor's and master's degrees from Texas Tech University and lives in Leander.

priorities.text: Lists public safety, infrastructure and responsible growth, long-term water security, and fiscal responsibility with low taxes as priorities.
Says the county's population is expected to double by 2050 and that roads and quality of life must keep pace.
Supports high school programs tied to local job needs.

record.text: Appointed county judge by a 3-1 Commissioners Court vote in March 2025 to serve until the November 2026 election.
Sponsored a $500,000 countywide water supply study, which he says covers both rural and city residents.
Says he led the court in approving large pay raises for Sheriff's deputies.
In 2025 the Commissioners Court he chairs adopted a FY2025-26 budget at the voter-approval tax rate of $0.413776, a 3.4% rate increase; Snell said residents should all be frustrated.
In September 2026 the court adopted a $712.9 million FY2026-27 budget at the no-new-revenue rate of $0.421547; Snell said he was happy to hold to the no-new-revenue rate.

notes.text: Unopposed in the March 2026 Republican primary.

q_water.summary: Sponsored a $500,000 county water supply study and calls long-term water security a key priority.

candidates.name: Ryan Guillen
candidates.current_role: Texas State Representative, District 31; chair of the House Homeland Security and Public Safety Committee
candidates.background: Ryan Guillen was elected to the Legislature at age 24. He holds an agriculture degree from Texas A&M University, worked as a high school agriculture teacher, and grew up working at his family's feed store and ranch. In 2025 he chaired the House Committee on Homeland Security and Public Safety.

photo.credit: Official portrait, Texas House of Representatives

priorities.text: His House biography describes him as an advocate for creating jobs, cutting taxes and red tape, and reducing over-testing.

record.text: Voted for SB 2 (2025), which created the state education savings account program, on its April 2025 House passage vote.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the House school finance and teacher pay bill.
Voted for the motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2 (2025), the final version of the school finance bill.
Was absent for the vote on SB 10 (2025), requiring display of the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms; a statement of vote in the journal says the member would have voted yes.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), the constitutional amendment allowing denial of bail for certain violent felony charges.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), changing bail procedures and regulating charitable bail organizations.
Voted for SB 3 (2025), which would have banned consumable hemp-derived THC products (later vetoed by the governor).
Voted for SB 17 (2025), restricting purchases of Texas land by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversary nations.
Voted for SB 8 (2025, regular session), requiring certain sheriffs to seek agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Voted for Amendment No. 22 to the 2025 budget (SB 1), which directed the state to seek a federal waiver to expand Medicaid eligibility; the amendment failed 63 to 85.
Voted for the 2026-27 state budget (SB 1) on House passage in April 2025.
Voted for SB 1362 (2025), prohibiting recognition and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders.
Voted for HB 7 (2025, second called session), allowing civil lawsuits over the manufacture and distribution of abortion-inducing drugs.
In the January 2025 runoff vote for Speaker, voted for David Cook over Dustin Burrows, who was elected Speaker.
In April 2023 voted yes on the motion to table, and no on adoption of, Amendment No. 45 to the budget, which barred state spending on vouchers or similar programs.
Voted against Amendment No. 2 to HB 1 (November 2023), which removed education savings accounts from the bill.
Voted for SB 14 (2023), prohibiting gender transition medical treatments for minors.
Voted for the 2023 motion to concur in Senate amendments to HB 2127, which limits city and county regulations in fields occupied by state law.
Voted for HR 2377 (May 2023), the articles of impeachment against Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was later acquitted by the Senate.
Voted for SB 3 (fourth called session, 2023), funding border barrier construction and border security operations.
Voted for SB 4 (fourth called session, 2023), creating a state criminal offense for illegal entry from a foreign nation.
Authored HB 101 (2025), creating the Texas State Guard Professionalization Task Force, and HB 2516 (2025), on Medicare supplement plans for people under 65; both became law.
Authored HJR 34 (2025), a property tax exemption constitutional amendment that was filed with the Secretary of State for voter approval, and filed border security bills including HB 176 and HB 246.
